whole.name: A master-worker batch job with re-execution and atomic output commit (MapReduce's master), run under a supervision tree with restart limits (Erlang/OTP)
whole.source: Dean, J. and Ghemawat, S. (2004), 'MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters', OSDI 2004 (master, task table, re-execution, atomic rename commit, semantics with non-deterministic operators). Armstrong, J. (2003), 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors', PhD thesis, KTH (supervisors, restart strategies, restart intensity, escalation).
whole.borrow: (1) A task table owned by the coordinator, kept as a file: one row per field with state (idle, in-progress, committed, failed), attempt number (epoch), session id, start time, spend and commit hash. (2) Re-execution on failure under a new attempt number, from the last checkpoint. (3) Atomic commit of an attempt's output: the attempt writes to fields/<f>/attempt-<e>/, and the commit is one atomic rename or a single-line COMMIT file naming the attempt and the hash. First commit wins. Later completions from stale attempts are ignored by the acceptor script. (4) The reduce (synthesis script) reads only committed attempts. (5) OTP restart intensity: at most R restarts per field and K across the tree in a period T, then escalate. (6) Master recovery from the task-table file (a fresh coordinator).

mappings.classical: Zombie processes and split brain after a failover: a process suspected dead resumes (after a pause, sleep or slow turn) and keeps writing after its replacement started. Solved by fencing.
solutions: Leases (time-bounded ownership) [Gray, C. and Cheriton, D. (1989), 'Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency', SOSP 1989]
Fencing by sequence number (sequencers) [Burrows, M. (2006), 'The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems', OSDI 2006]
mappings.rule: Each field and the coordinator carry an epoch number. Bumping the epoch fences the old incarnation. Only outputs stamped with the current epoch are accepted or merged.
mappings.runner: The watcher script bumps the epoch, and the coordinator starts the replacement. The acceptor and merge script (Node) enforces the epoch on every file it accepts.
mappings.on_failure: An output with epoch < EPOCH is rejected and logged to the ledger as a zombie write. A branch whose name has a stale epoch is never merged. If the EPOCH file cannot be written, no replacement starts and the watcher exits with 'fence-failed', which wakes the coordinator.
mappings.formula: replace(f): e := read EPOCH(f); write EPOCH(f) := e+1 atomically; mark the task-table row (f, e) as fenced; best-effort stop of the old session; start the new session with brief epoch=e+1 on branch child/f-e(e+1). accept(file): if file.epoch != read EPOCH(f), reject. The coordinator's own hand-over uses the same scheme on COORDINATOR_EPOCH: a woken coordinator whose epoch is stale ends its turn without acting.
mappings.fails_here: A session cannot be relied on to stop itself when its lease runs out: it has no clock between turns, sleep freezes it, and it can ignore an instruction. 'Stop before replacing' (STONITH in cluster practice) assumes the stop is confirmed, but a stop can fail silently, a sleeping PC resumes everything, and orphan helpers of a dead child keep running. When the holder cannot be trusted to stop, the field moves the check to the resource: fencing at the acceptor, not obedience at the writer.

mappings.classical: Failure detection in an asynchronous system: a slow process cannot be told apart from a dead one. Detectors are unreliable by nature and are tuned between detection time and the false-suspicion rate.
solutions: Unreliable failure detectors (completeness and accuracy classes) [Chandra, T.D. and Toueg, S. (1996), 'Unreliable failure detectors for reliable distributed systems', JACM 43(2)]
Phi accrual failure detector [Hayashibara, N., Defago, X., Yared, R. and Katayama, T. (2004), 'The phi accrual failure detector', SRDS 2004]
mappings.rule: Suspect a child when no progress event has arrived for longer than the measured distribution allows (phi above a threshold) or past a hard ceiling. Never suspect across a detected system pause.
mappings.runner: The watcher script (Node), one per wave
mappings.on_failure: Pause detected: reset every child's last-progress time to now, log 'pause' to the ledger, keep going. Child suspected: exit with code 'stall:<f>', which wakes the coordinator. The coordinator then uses the D1-01 replacement path, never a direct restart. If the watcher itself crashes, its exit still wakes the coordinator, and the coordinator treats a watcher crash as 'restart the watcher', not as a field failure.
mappings.formula: Pause detection: if (now - lastTick) > 2Δ + 30 s, then the system was paused, so do not suspect anyone. Progress events are distinct new source ids, new question ids covered, and new committed files whose hash differs from all earlier ones. The same card rewritten does not count. With μ = the mean interval between progress events measured on the pilot, under an exponential model φ(t) = t / (μ · ln 10), where t = time since the last progress event. Suspect when φ > Φ (Φ = 3 means about a 0.1 % chance that a healthy child is this quiet) or when t > T_max (a hard cap, for example 3μ, or the time box). A loop check also runs: if the last k = 5 events add no new source id or question id, suspect a loop even when files keep appearing.
mappings.fails_here: (1) The monitored signal is a liveness heartbeat in the classical case. Here liveness is worthless: a looping session is alive. The signal must be progress, and the current rule already says so. (2) 'New confirmed cards' cannot be the progress signal during research, because under P1 confirmation runs after the review. Use new distinct cards and increased question coverage instead. (3) Stationarity fails: a child reads for a long time, then writes in bursts. (4) PC sleep freezes the watcher too, and on wake every timer fires at once (a process pause). The field's answer to (3) is a hard upper bound beside the adaptive one. Its answer to (4) is to detect the pause and suspend suspicion.

mappings.classical: Crash-recovery with checkpoints and logs (rollback recovery), plus orphans: work done for a dead parent and lost with it.
solutions: Checkpointing and message logging (rollback-recovery) [Elnozahy, E.N., Alvisi, L., Wang, Y.-M. and Johnson, D.B. (2002), 'A survey of rollback-recovery protocols in message-passing systems', ACM Computing Surveys 34(3)]
Atomic commit of a task's output by rename [Dean, J. and Ghemawat, S. (2004), 'MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters', OSDI 2004]
mappings.rule: (a) Every file is written by temp file plus rename. A JSONL line is accepted only if it parses, and a truncated last line is dropped. (b) Each attempt writes under attempt-<epoch>/, and a COMMIT file makes it visible. (c) On restart, a salvage script pulls helper results (cards) out of the dead session's transcript into the new attempt's input before the fresh session starts. (d) Restart reads only committed or salvaged material.
mappings.runner: Writes: the child session, through a small Node helper write-atomic.js that it calls. Salvage: a Node script that the coordinator runs before every replacement. Acceptance: the acceptor script.
mappings.on_failure: A card salvaged from the transcript fails the schema: drop it and log it. The transcript is unreadable: restart from the last committed cards only, and log the lost helper count. A partial attempt folder without COMMIT is never read by the synthesis.
mappings.formula: Restart point = last COMMIT ∪ schema-valid cards salvaged from the transcript and deduplicated by source id. Lost work = helper results in the transcript − salvaged cards.
mappings.fails_here: Piecewise determinism fails: replaying a session's inputs does not give the same session. So the field's answer for non-deterministic processes applies: log the outputs (the effects), not the inputs, and restart from the last logged output rather than replaying. Helpers return their results only into the child's window (readers hold no write tools, by P5), so a child crash loses every in-flight card: the orphan problem. There is a log the session cannot forget to write: the harness's own transcript on disk, which records every helper result. That makes it a write-ahead log kept by the infrastructure, not by the session.

mappings.classical: Common-mode or correlated failure in redundant software: N-version programming and the failure of its independence assumption.
solutions: N-version programming (design diversity with voting) [Avizienis, A. (1985), 'The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-11(12)]

The experimental test of that assumption [Knight, J.C. and Leveson, N.G. (1986), 'An experimental evaluation of the assumption of independence in multiversion programming', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-12(1)]
Data diversity (re-expressed inputs to one program) [Ammann, P.E. and Knight, J.C. (1988), 'Data diversity: an approach to software fault tolerance', IEEE Transactions on Computers 37(4)]
mappings.rule: Agreement never raises a claim (as now). A second opinion is worth its cost only if it differs in inputs (a different source set: the contrary-evidence reader of P16) or in kind (a different model, or a deterministic check). A second same-model run on the same inputs is not bought.
mappings.runner: The coordinator, when it chooses the F2 form; the synthesis script, which ignores agreement counts
mappings.on_failure: If no diverse input or model is available, the claim stays at single-reading strength and is marked so. It is never upgraded.
mappings.formula: Under correlation ρ between two readers' errors with error rate p, P(both wrong) ≈ p² + ρ·p(1−p). At ρ near 1 a second reader adds nothing. Estimate ρ on the pilot as the co-error rate on cards that the checker found wrong.
mappings.fails_here: Independence fails even more than in Knight and Leveson: two instances of one model share weights, training data and blind spots. What the field does when design diversity cannot be had is two things. Do not count agreement as masking. Get diversity from inputs (data diversity) or from a verifier of a different kind (D1-05).

mappings.classical: Byzantine faults (a component answers wrongly, possibly convincingly). Two families of solutions: replication with voting (which needs independence, see D1-04), or authenticated, verifiable messages that any receiver checks for itself.
solutions: Byzantine Generals: oral messages (3f+1) versus signed messages (any number of traitors) [Lamport, L., Shostak, R. and Pease, M. (1982), 'The Byzantine Generals Problem', ACM TOPLAS 4(3)]
Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (replicated state machine) [Castro, M. and Liskov, B. (1999), 'Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance', OSDI 1999]
mappings.rule: Every card carries the snapshot hash of the page text it quotes. A claim is 'verified' only if a script finds the exact quote (after whitespace and Unicode normalisation) in that snapshot and the number in or next to the quote. A model checker judges only conditions and citing-sentence scope, and its verdict is labelled as a judgment.
mappings.runner: A Node script, quote-check.js. It fetches the page once with Node's built-in fetch, stores the bytes under sources/<sha256>, and runs the match. The checker agent handles judgment only.
mappings.on_failure: Quote not found, or page not fetchable: the card is 'unverified' and may not support a conclusion; the citing sentence is struck or marked as judgment; the ledger counts it. PDF or JavaScript-rendered pages that plain Node cannot turn into text are marked 'unverifiable by script', never silently passed.
mappings.formula: verified(card) := sha256(snapshot) = card.snapshot_hash ∧ normalise(card.quote) ⊂ normalise(text(snapshot)) ∧ card.number appears within w = 300 characters of the quote.
mappings.fails_here: PBFT's replica independence fails (D1-04), so the replicated route is closed. The signed-message route maps: a claim that carries a verifiable link to its evidence (source snapshot hash, exact quote, number) can be checked by a deterministic verifier that is not a model, so it is immune to shared blind spots. The step that is not deterministic, 'the citing sentence stays within the card's conditions' (P17), is a judgment. For that step the field has no masking answer without independence: label it as judgment and keep its error rate in the ledger.

mappings.classical: Where to put the correctness check in a multi-hop path: the end-to-end argument.
solutions: End-to-end arguments [Saltzer, J.H., Reed, D.P. and Clark, D.D. (1984), 'End-to-end arguments in system design', ACM TOCS 2(4)]
mappings.rule: The final artifact (the synthesis and the owner's page) is itself checked: every factual sentence resolves through card ids to a verified card (D1-05), and every number in the sentence equals the card's number with the same unit and conditions tag. Hop-by-hop checks stay as early warnings.
mappings.runner: A Node script, e2e-check.js, run by the coordinator
mappings.on_failure: Any sentence that fails is struck or marked 'unchecked judgment'. If more than x % fail, the synthesis is not released and the coordinator is woken.
mappings.formula: For each sentence s with numbers N(s) and cited cards C(s): pass iff C(s) is not empty, every c in C(s) is verified, and every n in N(s) matches some c.number (equal after unit normalisation).
mappings.fails_here: Few. The endpoint here is the owner's page and the synthesis, not the review. The current check sits one hop early: the synthesis and the owner page are further hops where a condition can fall off or a number be retyped.

mappings.classical: Effects that must happen exactly once (starting a costly child, merging, freezing a pack, ledger entries, a message to the owner) under retries and restarts: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects, through intent records.
solutions: Idempotence keys [Helland, P. (2012), 'Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition', ACM Queue 10(4) (also CACM 55(5))]
Entities and activities without distributed transactions [Helland, P. (2007), 'Life beyond Distributed Transactions: an Apostate's Opinion', CIDR 2007]
mappings.rule: Every costly or external effect has a key (field, epoch, step). An intent record is created exclusively before the effect. After any restart, intents are reconciled against reality before anything is redone.
mappings.runner: The coordinator, through a Node script intent.js (fs.openSync(path,'wx') is an atomic exclusive create); the ledger merge script deduplicates by (session_id, seq)
mappings.on_failure: The create fails because the file exists: the effect may have happened, so the coordinator checks reality (a session with that name, a merged commit, a hash file) and does not repeat it blindly. A merge is naturally idempotent (git merge of an already-merged commit is a no-op). Ledger lines with a repeated key are dropped.
mappings.formula: do(effect, key): if create_exclusive(intent(key)) fails, then reconcile(key) and return. Otherwise perform(effect); write done(key). On restart, for every intent without done: if observed(effect) then write done, else perform again (safe only because of the epoch fence, D1-01).
mappings.fails_here: The coordinator may die between deciding and recording a session start (it cannot do both atomically), and the session list is the only ground truth about whether a start happened. The field's answer: write the intent before the effect, then reconcile the intent against the observed world after a restart.

mappings.classical: Admission control with budget reservation (escrow), bounded concurrency, and back-pressure; a barrier compared with work-conserving scheduling.
solutions: Escrow transactional method [O'Neil, P.E. (1986), 'The escrow transactional method', ACM TODS 11(4)]
Little's law for sizing concurrency and time [Little, J.D.C. (1961), 'A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW', Operations Research 9(3)]
mappings.rule: Each field is admitted individually, when a slot is free, if the unreserved budget covers its escrow. The escrow is reserved at start and released at commit. The watcher stops a field at its escrow. The coordinator reads the true meter at each wake and corrects the remaining budget.
mappings.runner: Admission and escrow: the coordinator, using admit.js over the task table. Enforcement: the watcher, using spend from transcripts. True meter: the coordinator (get_usage).
mappings.on_failure: Not admitted: the field stays idle and is reported, never started 'to see'. Over escrow: the watcher exits 'overspend:<f>', and the coordinator freezes the field (pack cut to its limit, rest 'not covered'), no top-up without the owner. Meter and transcript count disagree by more than 20 %: stop admitting and wake the coordinator.
mappings.formula: Escrow e_f = (1+m) · ĉ · q_f / q_pilot. Admit f iff B − Σ(open escrows) − r ≥ e_f and running < N (N = 2 or 3 by free memory). After each committed field, update ĉ to the mean cost per question so far and m to max(m_owner, 2·s/ĉ), where s is the observed standard deviation (needs at least 3 fields; before that, the owner's m). Expected wall time ≈ (F/N)·W̄, by Little's law with a work-conserving queue, against Σ over waves of max W_f with barriers.
mappings.fails_here: A child's draw is not known in advance (P14), and the only meter a script can read is token counts from transcripts, not the plan's meter. The field's answer is to reserve an estimate with a margin, enforce it at the consumer (the watcher exits on overspend), and reconcile against the true meter at the coordinator's turns. A sample of one pilot gives no variance, so the margin is a guess until more fields have run; update it after each field (an estimate that improves as it runs). Waves of three are a barrier: a wave waits for its slowest field, and slots stay idle.

mappings.classical: Supervision with restart limits and escalation (restart intensity); distinguishing a local fault from a common cause.
solutions: Supervision trees, restart strategies and restart intensity [Armstrong, J. (2003), 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors', PhD thesis, Royal Institute of Technology (KTH), Stockholm]
mappings.rule: Per field: at most R_f = 1 automatic replacement (from checkpoint, D1-03), then the field is failed and escalated to the owner with its ledger. Tree-wide: if two or more children fail within the same window W (for example 30 min), treat it as a common cause. Stop all admission, restart nothing, wake the coordinator with 'common-cause'.
mappings.runner: The watcher (counts failures and time) and the coordinator (decides)
mappings.on_failure: Escalation goes to the owner: the coordinator writes a status line and stops the wave. It never retries past the limit.
mappings.formula: failures_f ≥ R_f + 1 ⇒ fail field f. |{f : failed in [t−W, t]}| ≥ 2 ⇒ common cause ⇒ halt admission.
mappings.fails_here: A restart costs a large token amount, not milliseconds, so R must be small. Many faults here are not transient: a bad brief or a bad pack fails the same way again. Common-cause faults (allowance exhausted, reboot, sleep, the fetch tool down) hit every child at once, and restarting each one separately is exactly what OTP's one_for_all and escalation exist to prevent.

mappings.classical: Bounding the state of a long-running leader: snapshots plus log truncation, and a leader whose decisions are a function of persistent state (state machine approach).
solutions: Snapshotting and log compaction [Ongaro, D. and Ousterhout, J. (2014), 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm', USENIX ATC 2014]
State machine approach [Schneider, F.B. (1990), 'Implementing fault-tolerant services using the state machine approach: a tutorial', ACM Computing Surveys 22(4)]
mappings.rule: status.json is generated by a script from the task table, intents and files. It is the snapshot. A coordinator decision is a log entry (decisions.jsonl) with an id. The hand-over at 200,000 tokens bumps COORDINATOR_EPOCH (D1-01) and restarts the watchers under the new coordinator, so the wake-up goes to the live one.
mappings.runner: status.js (Node), run by the watcher on each tick and by the coordinator on wake; the handing-over coordinator for the epoch bump
mappings.on_failure: status.js fails: the coordinator does not act on memory; it stops and reports. A stale coordinator woken after hand-over sees the epoch mismatch and ends its turn.
mappings.formula: next_actions = f(status) is deterministic: admit (D1-08), replace (D1-01, D1-09), accept (D1-05), release. The session's window holds only status.json, the last N decisions and verdict files.
mappings.fails_here: The coordinator is not deterministic. So split it: a deterministic part (a script that computes state and the next legal actions from the task table and files) and a judgment part (the session). Only the deterministic part's output is the snapshot. The coordinator's own summary is not, because a self-written summary is not a faithful image (the current rule already points at the status file; keep it).

mappings.classical: Duplicate work across workers. Two standard answers: avoid coordination and accept duplicates (safe when work is idempotent), or claim work atomically. The withdrawn register failed because it used check-then-act, the classic race, not because claiming is wrong.
solutions: Coordination avoidance (invariant confluence) [Bailis, P., Fekete, A., Franklin, M.J., Ghodsi, A., Hellerstein, J.M. and Stoica, I. (2014), 'Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems', PVLDB 8(3)]
Conflict-free replicated data types (grow-only set) [Shapiro, M., Preguica, N., Baquero, C. and Zawirski, M. (2011), 'Conflict-free Replicated Data Types', SSS 2011]
mappings.rule: Keep the current rule: no coordination, overlap counted. Optional upgrade if the pilot shows overlap is costly: a content-addressed card cache, sources/<sha256(canonical url or DOI)>/card.json. The first writer wins by exclusive create, and a later field reads and reuses that card (adding its own field tag in its own folder) instead of re-reading.
mappings.runner: The child (it has write tools; readers do not) calls cache.js before dispatching a reader; the overlap counter script runs after each wave
mappings.on_failure: Exclusive create fails: read the existing card. If it is unparseable, read the source anyway (at-least-once). Never block on another field.
mappings.formula: Build the cache only if overlap_rate × mean reader cost × remaining fields exceeds the build cost. overlap_rate = |sources read by ≥2 fields| / |sources read|.
mappings.fails_here: A card is shaped partly by its field's question, so a 'claimed' paper must not be withheld from a neighbour. Deduplicate the reading (cache), not the use.

mappings.classical: A recovery path that is rarely exercised is broken when it is needed. Crash-only design makes recovery the normal path.
solutions: Crash-only software [Candea, G. and Fox, A. (2003), 'Crash-Only Software', HotOS IX]
mappings.rule: Whatever F1 decides on quality, the fresh-from-frozen-pack path must run at least once in the pilot as a real path, so that the crash and full-window path is known to work.
mappings.runner: The coordinator, in the pilot
mappings.on_failure: If the fresh path fails, recovery is not available, and the tree may not start further fields until it is fixed.
mappings.formula: None.
mappings.fails_here: Recovery here is not cheap: a fresh reviewer re-reads the pack. The field argues only about dependability, not about review quality, which is outside this field.

mappings.classical: Completeness of a failure analysis: enumerate a fault model (failure classes) against every component, rather than collecting risks from memory.
solutions: Failure semantics taxonomy (crash, omission, timing, response or arbitrary failures) [Cristian, F. (1991), 'Understanding fault-tolerant distributed systems', Communications of the ACM 34(2)]
mappings.rule: A table of components × {crash, crash-recovery with amnesia, omission (lost output or message), timing (too slow or too fast), wrong answer (Byzantine), common-cause}. Every cell names the problem id that covers it, or 'gap'. The list counts as complete for the fault model when no cell says 'gap'.
mappings.runner: The coordinator writes it once; a refuter attacks the cells marked covered
mappings.on_failure: A gap cell becomes a new problem id or an accepted risk with the owner's word
mappings.formula: 13 components × 6 classes = 78 cells.
mappings.fails_here: The component list itself is the weak point. Include non-obvious components: the fetch tool, the usage meter, the PC power state, the owner (a slow or absent approver), the transcript files, git, and the scripts themselves.

missing.title: A zombie writes after its replacement started
missing.classical: Split brain / zombie process (needs fencing)
missing.mechanism: Epoch numbers checked by the acceptor and merge script (D1-01).

missing.title: Every timer fires after the PC wakes from sleep
missing.classical: Process pause / clock jump causing mass false suspicion
missing.mechanism: Detect a tick gap greater than 2Δ + 30 s, reset suspicion and log a pause (D1-02).

missing.title: One cause fails every session at once
missing.classical: Common-mode (correlated) failure
missing.mechanism: Two or more failures within a window ⇒ halt admission and escalate (D1-09).

missing.title: Restarts use up the budget that would have let work finish
missing.classical: Retry storm / metastable failure (Bronson, N., Aghayev, A., Charapko, A. and Zhu, T. (2021), 'Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems', HotOS 2021)
missing.mechanism: Restart intensity limits, restart from checkpoint, and escrow (D1-03, D1-08, D1-09).

missing.title: Half-written files, or outputs of two attempts mixed
missing.classical: Torn writes; non-atomic commit
missing.mechanism: Write by temp file plus rename, attempt folders, and a COMMIT file that the synthesis reads exclusively (D1-03).

missing.title: The wake-up goes to nobody
missing.classical: Lost wake-up / unsupervised supervisor (who watches the watcher)
missing.mechanism: Watchers restart under every new coordinator epoch. The watcher carries its own hard deadline (process.exit after T_max) and writes a tick line to status.json; the coordinator checks the tick age on every wake. After a reboot nothing runs until the owner, or a logon task he approves, starts a fresh coordinator.

missing.title: Helpers keep running for a dead child, and their results are lost
missing.classical: Orphan computations
missing.mechanism: Salvage from the transcript (D1-03); orphans are counted in the ledger.

missing.title: Files keep appearing but nothing is learned
missing.classical: Gray failure (Huang, P. et al. (2017), 'Gray Failure: The Achilles' Heel of Cloud-Scale Systems', HotOS 2017): healthy to the monitor's own check, failing for its users
missing.mechanism: Progress = new distinct source ids and new question ids covered; a loop test over the last k events (D1-02).

missing.classical: Straggler at a barrier (bulk-synchronous waves against work-conserving scheduling)
missing.mechanism: Admit per field as slots free, subject to escrow (D1-08).

missing.title: A costly effect happens twice
missing.classical: Duplicate side effects under retry (lack of idempotence)
missing.mechanism: Intent records by exclusive create, reconciled after restart (D1-07).

do_not: Do not treat agreement among instances of the same model as a Byzantine quorum or as N-version masking: the independence assumption is false (Knight and Leveson 1986).
Do not use liveness (alive, answering, writing files) as evidence of progress, and do not count rewrites as progress.
Do not start a replacement on a timeout without fencing the old incarnation at the acceptor; a 'stop' that cannot be confirmed is not a fence.
Do not check-then-act on a shared file. Use one writer, an atomic exclusive create (fs.openSync with 'wx') or an atomic rename.

Do not build consensus, distributed locks or two-phase commit across sessions. One coordinator, epochs and idempotent effects are enough on one PC, and a blocking coordinator protocol would stall on a sleeping session.
Do not retry without a limit, and do not restart all failed children separately after a common-cause failure; cap restarts and escalate.
Do not let wall-clock timeouts run across sleep or a pause without detecting the pause.
Do not let the synthesis read uncommitted or mixed attempts.
Do not borrow speculative backup tasks for stragglers: they double the token cost.
Do not let a component's self-report be the measure of its own health or spend; measure it from outside (transcripts, files).
Do not treat a fixed time box chosen by guess as a failure detector; measure the progress interval in the pilot.
result.check_overall: All 24 citations name real works with correct authors, years and venues. This rests on web searches for only three items (MapReduce semantics, Chubby sequencers, Armstrong's restart rule) and my recall of the standard records for the rest, which I did not fetch. Three claims are overstated. First, MapReduce's non-deterministic guarantee is per reduce task, so it does not give a job-wide single-execution guarantee. Second, Chubby sequencers are validated against Chubby or the server's cache, not by a plain monotonic-number check. Third, the thesis was not confirmed to state restart intensity; OTP documentation does. Minor softening is also needed for Helland 2012 and phi accrual.

whole.name: An append-only, multi-version database with a staging area: per-writer write-ahead logs, atomic commit of each unit, immutable copy-on-write versions read as snapshots, declared integrity constraints checked at commit, and derived data kept as materialized views with lineage
whole.source: Mohan, Haderle, Lindsay, Pirahesh, Schwarz 1992, ARIES (ACM TODS 17(1)); Bernstein and Goodman 1983, Multiversion Concurrency Control: Theory and Algorithms (ACM TODS 8(4)); Codd 1970, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (CACM 13(6)); Gupta and Mumick 1995, Maintenance of Materialized Views: Problems, Techniques, and Applications (IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin 18(2)); Gray and Reuter 1993, Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques
whole.borrow: Six parts carry over whole. (1) The commit protocol: stage, then validate with schema and constraints, then publish atomically (temp file, rename, then a journal line). An output with no journal line does not exist. (2) Value logging: log the produced card or section itself, never the brief that produced it. (3) Immutable versions: a pack repair is a new version with a new hash, and every review, certificate and status line names the hash it read. (4) Foreign keys with a declared delete action: a dropped card cascades to stale on every sentence, claim and certificate that depends on it. (5) Normalised storage: each fact is stored once in its card, and every other place it appears is rendered from the card by a script. (6) Readers of published results see committed data only.

mappings.classical: Building a balanced index over a key set known in advance: bulk loading at a chosen fill factor, with node capacity and partitioning by key range
solutions: B-tree, B+ tree (data in the leaves, separator keys in the inner nodes) [Bayer and McCreight 1972, Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes, Acta Informatica 1(3); Comer 1979, The Ubiquitous B-Tree, ACM Computing Surveys 11(2)]
Bulk loading at a fill factor [Practitioner standard (for example, PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX with fillfactor; the B-tree leaf default is 90). I am not sure of a single original paper]
Expected occupancy under random growth [Yao 1978, On Random 2-3 Trees, Acta Informatica 9]
mappings.rule: Fields are bulk-loaded from the approved question ids. The ids are ordered by mechanism tag, so that each range is one coherent expertise. Consecutive ranges are assigned to fields until each field's estimated load reaches f times C. A field whose estimate exceeds f times C is split by question range at plan time, and the split goes to the owner as an amendment before any research starts. The current design has no packing step: fields come from the lanes, and their size is checked only after the work is spent.
mappings.runner: A Node planning script that the coordinator runs. The output table goes to the owner.
mappings.on_failure: A question with no estimate is not packed. It is listed instead, and no wave may start while its plan has unpacked ids.
mappings.formula: est(field) = sum of t_q over the questions in the field. Greedy packing in mechanism order while est(field) <= f*C. Number of fields >= ceil(sum over all q of t_q / (f*C)). Start f at about 0.7 to 0.8: near Yao's 0.69 for random growth, leaving room for the one repair, the contrary-evidence reader and the re-checks. Retune f to the slack actually used.
mappings.fails_here: Four fail. (1) The cost of a key is neither uniform nor known in advance: one question can cost ten times another, and that is known only after it is spent. (2) Keys are not independent: questions that share a mechanism share their reading, so cutting a range loses shared context, which a B+ separator never does. (3) A full window cannot be split in O(node); splitting it means redoing the research. (4) The tree has seven leaves and one inner node, so the height and log properties add nothing. What survives is capacity, fill factor and partitioning by key range. The field's answer when key sizes are unknown is to sample statistics first, which here is the pilot, then load with slack.

mappings.classical: A node that overflows: split at insert time, redistribution to a sibling, out-of-line (overflow) storage, sibling links under concurrent access, copy-on-write versions
solutions: Split at insert time by key [Bayer and McCreight 1972, Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes, Acta Informatica 1(3)]
Redistribution before splitting (B*-tree) [Knuth 1973, The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 3: Sorting and Searching]
Out-of-line storage for large values (overflow pages, TOAST) [Practitioner standard (for example, PostgreSQL TOAST)]
Sibling links with a high key (B-link tree) [Lehman and Yao 1981, Efficient Locking for Concurrent Operations on B-Trees, ACM TODS 6(4)]
Copy-on-write (shadowing) [Lorie 1977, Physical Integrity in a Large Segmented Database, ACM TODS 2(1); Rodeh 2008, B-trees, Shadowing, and Clones, ACM Transactions on Storage]
mappings.rule: Judgement of the present rule: 'cut the pack to its limit and list the rest as not covered' agrees with the standard in that the uncovered keys stay visible. It runs against the standard in that confirmed, paid-for data is dropped from the reviewer's view, which a B+ tree never does. Replace it by separating two overflows. (a) Research overflow, when the questions do not fit the child's budget. Before each question group the child runs a capacity check. If the group would not fit, the child stops inserting and writes an overflow record {question ids, tokens used, reason}. The coordinator then moves that range to a field in the same wave that has slack (redistribution), or schedules it as an overflow field at the next wave's admission. (b) Pack overflow, when the pack exceeds what a reviewer may read. The pack becomes a two-level index: for each mechanism, a bounded summary plus card ids. All confirmed cards stay in cards.jsonl and are read by id on demand. Nothing confirmed is cut. (c) Every pack revision is written as a new file named by its hash, and old versions are never edited (copy-on-write).
mappings.runner: The child runs the capacity-check script before each question group. The watcher exits on an overflow record. The coordinator decides redistribution or deferral. The pack schema check enforces the per-mechanism bound.
mappings.on_failure: If no estimate exists or the check errors, treat it as an overflow: stop inserting and wake the coordinator. An overflow range that is neither scheduled nor dropped by name by the owner blocks the synthesis gate. It then appears in the synthesis as 'not covered', with its reason.
mappings.formula: Insert allowed iff U + sum over the next range of t_q <= (1 - r)*C, where U is tokens used and r is the reserve for the review. r is non-zero only if F1 keeps the review in the same window; it is that review's measured token need. Redistribution target: the sibling in the wave with the most slack (f*C - est); split or defer only when no sibling has slack >= est(range). Pack: summary bound per mechanism = B/m for a total bound B and m mechanisms; card bodies are out of line.
mappings.fails_here: In a B+ tree the split is triggered by the one insert that does not fit, and it costs one node copy. Here the 'data' is research already paid for, held in a window that cannot be divided. That is why the withdrawn rule failed: it split after the fact, when the full node had been built at full cost, and it split the content (the pack) instead of the key range (the question ids). The idea of splitting was sound. Its timing and its key were wrong. Sibling links pay off only under many concurrent operations. With seven fields and three sessions they are analogy only: a one-line forward pointer in a field's status, when a range moves, is all that is worth borrowing.

mappings.classical: Crash recovery: write-ahead logging, an atomic commit point per unit of work, torn writes, restart from a checkpoint plus the log tail
solutions: ARIES (write-ahead logging; restart in three passes: analysis, redo, undo) [Mohan, Haderle, Lindsay, Pirahesh, Schwarz 1992, ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging, ACM TODS 17(1)]
Transaction processing: atomicity and durability through logging [Gray and Reuter 1993, Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques]
mappings.rule: Every durable output is committed through one script: validate the schema, write a temp file, rename it into place, then append a journal line {seq, kind, path, sha256, question ids} to the session's own journal. An output with no journal line does not exist. At each pack freeze the folder is committed to the child's branch; that commit is the checkpoint. Restart is a recovery script. It reads the journal, verifies the hashes, and copies a torn last line to .corrupt and drops it. It then computes done (the committed items) and todo (the approved ids minus done), and briefs the fresh session from the latest frozen pack, the committed items after it, and the todo list. The present 'one path' rule is checkpoint-only. It does not define a commit point per unit, does not replay the log tail after the freeze, and does not guard against a half-written file.
mappings.runner: The child calls the commit script for each card or section. The coordinator or the watcher runs the recovery script before any replacement session starts.
mappings.on_failure: On a hash mismatch or an unparseable journal, the script exits non-zero, nothing restarts, and the coordinator wakes. No replacement starts until the old session is confirmed stopped, because two writers on one journal is the failure WAL forbids.
mappings.formula: Work lost on a crash is at most one uncommitted unit (one card or one section), plus whatever the window read but never committed. Restart cost = the fresh session's fixed prefix + the checkpoint (pack) + the log tail after it.
mappings.fails_here: Redo by re-running a brief is not deterministic: a rerun gives different cards. The field's answer is value logging, which records the after-image (the card or section itself) and never the intent. Sessions are also not fail-stop: a session can commit a confident wrong card before it dies. Logging makes that card durable, not true; truth stays with the checker. A sleep or a reboot is a crash. A rename within one NTFS volume serves as the atomic publish step.

mappings.classical: The cost of replaying a log that keeps growing: checkpointing and log truncation, the optimum checkpoint interval, and a checkpoint taken from the system rather than written by hand
solutions: Checkpoints bound redo to the log after the checkpoint [Mohan et al. 1992, ARIES, ACM TODS 17(1)]
Optimum checkpoint interval [Young 1974, A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval, Communications of the ACM 17(9)]
mappings.rule: A script regenerates the status file at every coordinator turn from the merged ledgers, journals and gate results; the coordinator never writes it by hand. The coordinator hands over at a threshold W* computed from measured growth and hand-over cost, not at a fixed 200,000. The successor reads only the protocol and the status file.
mappings.runner: The watcher computes the coordinator's current input tokens from its transcript and exits with 'handover' at W*. The coordinator then starts its successor.
mappings.on_failure: If the status regeneration fails, there is no hand-over and no new wave, and the coordinator wakes with the error. If the successor reads beyond the status file to orient itself, the checkpoint is lossy; the ledger records this, and the missing field is added to the status script.
mappings.formula: Input on call i = P + g*i, where P is the fixed prefix including the status file and g the tokens added per turn. One epoch of k turns costs k*P + g*k^2/2 + H. Per turn: H/k + P + g*k/2, minimised at k* = sqrt(2H/g). Threshold W* = P + g*k*. Count tokens and cost separately: cached reads cost less but count the same in the owner's token measure. If k* comes out small, the coordinator should be close to stateless per turn, which is what 'reads status files only' intends.
mappings.fails_here: Young trades checkpoint cost against work lost to failures. Here the trade is the cost of a hand-over against the cost of re-reading a growing window on every call. The square-root shape is the same, but the quantities differ, so the formula below is derived here, not borrowed. A database checkpoint is complete by construction. A hand-over note that the coordinator writes is a lossy self-summary. The field's fix is to make the status a view computed from the logs.

mappings.classical: Write-write conflicts and lost updates, avoided by partitioned (shared-nothing) ownership, with per-writer logs merged in a defined order
solutions: Shared-nothing partitioning [Stonebraker 1986, The Case for Shared Nothing, IEEE Database Engineering Bulletin 9(1)]
mappings.rule: One writer per folder, a worktree per child, and only the coordinator merges. This is shared-nothing partitioning, and it stands. Add enforcement: the merge script refuses any child branch whose diff touches paths outside that child's folder. Each ledger line carries (session id, per-session seq), and the merge orders by those; wall-clock time is kept for information only.
mappings.runner: The coordinator's merge script.
mappings.on_failure: The merge is refused, the offending paths are listed, and the coordinator wakes.
mappings.formula: Accept iff every path in the diff starts with the child's folder. Merged ledger = the union sorted by (session id, seq), with no clock comparison across sessions.
mappings.fails_here: Nothing enforces the partition except discipline: a session with write tools can write anywhere. Ledger lines merged by wall-clock time are misordered across a sleep or a reboot, or when two sessions' clocks disagree.

mappings.classical: Duplicate work under concurrency: insert-if-absent on a unique key, and the choice between pessimistic claims and optimistic validation at commit
solutions: Optimistic concurrency control (a read phase, then validation, then the write) [Kung and Robinson 1981, On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control, ACM TODS 6(2)]
Unique key with an atomic insert-if-absent (exclusive create) [Practitioner standard: a unique constraint in SQL; O_CREAT|O_EXCL in POSIX, the 'wx' flag in Node]
mappings.rule: 'Accepted and counted' is optimistic concurrency control whose validation step takes no action. Give the validation an action without a shared writable file. Cards are keyed by a canonical source key: a normalised DOI, an arXiv id, or a normalised URL. At each merge, the coordinator's merge script, as the only writer, folds the new cards into a merged card store. A second card on an existing key is kept as a second reading of that source, and its number, baseline and conditions are compared with the first. A disagreement flags both cards for the checker, so duplicates become free re-reads (correlated, since it is the same model). From the second wave on, the merged store is read-only input: before sending a reader to a source, the child looks up its key and reuses the card if one exists. Within a wave, overlap is accepted (optimistic); across waves, it is removed by lookup. Switch to pessimistic claims only if the measured overlap makes them pay.
mappings.runner: The coordinator's merge script (dedupe and compare); the child's lookup script before it dispatches a reader.
mappings.on_failure: An unparseable or unkeyable card (no canonical key) is refused at merge and returned to its child. Disagreeing duplicates go to the checker queue.
mappings.formula: Choose pessimistic claims within a wave iff overlap_rate * t_read > t_claim_round, where overlap_rate is the within-wave duplicate share per source, t_read the tokens of a reader on one source, and t_claim_round the extra tokens and time of a search-then-claim round per source.
mappings.fails_here: The withdrawal gave 'check-then-claim races' as its reason. That is not a reason: an atomic exclusive create removes the race. The real costs of a register here are different. Readers hold no write tools (P5), so they cannot claim anything. Readers discover sources while they search, so a pessimistic claim needs an extra round: search, then claim, then read. And a claim must not block a neighbouring field that needs the same paper; the field's answer is read-through, reusing the stored row instead of blocking.

mappings.classical: Referential integrity between reviews and the cards they cite; lineage (why-provenance); invalidating derived data when a base row changes
solutions: Keys and foreign keys, with a declared action on delete [Codd 1970, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks, Communications of the ACM 13(6); the SQL standard's referential actions]
Why- and where-provenance [Buneman, Khanna, Tan 2001, Why and Where: A Characterization of Data Provenance, ICDT]
Maintenance of materialized views [Gupta and Mumick 1995, Maintenance of Materialized Views: Problems, Techniques, and Applications, IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin 18(2)]
mappings.rule: Store the data as JSONL relations: cards; card_status (append-only); sentences {id, review, approach_id, measure, kind fact|judgment, declared scope: task, model, repository size, and so on, from fixed vocabularies}; cites {sentence_id, card_id, pack_hash}; claims (synthesis); derives {claim_id, sentence_id}. The check script enforces five constraints. Every fact sentence has at least one cite. Every cite resolves to a card in the named pack version. The cited card's status is confirmed. The sentence's declared scope lies within the card's conditions, field by field (a CHECK). When a card's status turns to dropped or corrected, every dependent sentence, claim and certificate is marked stale (cascade to stale, never delete). A certificate (P13) is the constraint set evaluated over one named snapshot hash, and it is void once that snapshot changes. The present rule checks once, after the review, and says nothing about what a later failure does to the review, the synthesis or the certificate.
mappings.runner: The schema and check script.
mappings.on_failure: The gate refuses any artifact with a dangling or stale dependency or a failed scope CHECK. The stale list goes to the owning child for repair, and the coordinator wakes.
mappings.formula: stale(X) = the transitive closure of the dependents of the changed cards over the edges cites and derives. Scope check: for each field k of the declared scope, sentence.scope[k] must be among card.conditions[k], or the sentence is flagged.
mappings.fails_here: A model writing a sentence from cards is not a query. Its lineage is only what it declares, the citation, and that can be incomplete: a sentence may rest on an uncited card or on the model's own memory. Integrity constraints catch dangling, stale and out-of-scope references. They cannot catch a false sentence that cites a valid card for something the card does not say, so the semantic check of P17 stays with the checker.

mappings.classical: Update anomalies from redundant copies: normalisation (each fact stored once), with derived copies generated by the system rather than maintained by hand
solutions: Normal forms (store each fact once; join to present it) [Codd 1970, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks, CACM 13(6); Codd 1972, Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model, in R. Rustin (ed.), Data Base Systems, Prentice-Hall]
mappings.rule: 'A card's conditions are copied field by field' is standard only if a script does the copying, in which case the copy is a materialized view. If a model retypes the fields, the rule runs against the standard. Models write references only: a card id, the sentence, and its declared scope. Numbers, baselines and conditions are never retyped. review.md, the synthesis page and the owner's page are rendered by a script that joins sentences to cards. Any number in model-written prose must equal a number in one of its cited cards, or the script flags it.
mappings.runner: The render script.
mappings.on_failure: Rendering refuses on a dangling reference. A flagged number sends its sentence to the checker queue.
mappings.formula: Rendered(sentence) = sentence JOIN cites JOIN cards on card_id; projection of the condition fields. Number check: extract numbers from the prose; each must match one of the cited cards' numbers, with a tolerance only for stated rounding.
mappings.fails_here: Here the copies are typed by models. Every retyped number, baseline or condition is a chance to drop or distort it, and that is exactly the hand-over loss. Denormalising by hand is the failure the field warns against.

mappings.classical: Non-repeatable reads of a source that changes or is read unfaithfully; read consistency from snapshots of stored versions
solutions: Isolation phenomena: non-repeatable read and phantom [Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil, O'Neil 1995, A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, SIGMOD]
Multiversion concurrency control (snapshot reads) [Bernstein and Goodman 1983, Multiversion Concurrency Control: Theory and Algorithms, ACM TODS 8(4)]
mappings.rule: When a card is committed, a Node script fetches the page bytes itself, extracts the text, and stores it under its content hash in a local cache outside git, because the copies are of others' works. It records the snapshot hash in the card and searches for the card's quote (with whitespace and case normalised) in that text. Checkers and the post-review check read the snapshot, never a fresh fetch through the summarising tool. A card with no snapshot, or whose quote is not found, has status 'unverified' and cannot be cited in a conclusion. The proposed F5 script is the right core; this adds storing the snapshot and pinning it to the card, so that the check reads the same version the reader saw.
mappings.runner: The commit script (D2-03) calls the snapshot script.
mappings.on_failure: A fetch failure, paywall, bot block or PDF that cannot be extracted makes the card 'unverified', listed for the owner. A card is never 'confirmed' without a snapshot.
mappings.formula: card.snapshot = sha256(extracted text). quote_found = normalise(quote) is a substring of normalise(text). Drift test on a sample: re-fetch at check time; if the hash differs from the snapshot, record it as drift.
mappings.fails_here: The web keeps no versions for us: pages change, vanish, block bots or serve different content to different requests. And the fetch tool returns a small model's summary instead of the page, an unfaithful read. The field's answer is to own the versioning: take a snapshot at read time and have every later check read that snapshot.

mappings.classical: Dirty reads and cascading aborts: whether readers may use uncommitted data (schedules that are recoverable, avoid cascading aborts, or are strict)
solutions: Schedules that avoid cascading aborts (read only committed data), and strict schedules [Bernstein, Hadzilacos, Goodman 1987, Concurrency Control and Recovery in Database Systems, Addison-Wesley]
The dirty-read phenomenon [Berenson et al. 1995, A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, SIGMOD]
mappings.rule: A review may cite only cards whose status is confirmed in the pack version it names. Cards behind the pack's conclusions are checked at freeze, when those conclusions exist (a strict schedule for the pack). Cards cited only by the review are checked after it (optimistic), and a failure cascades to stale through D2-07. Amendment 3 moved every check after the review; that is the optimistic choice, and it is sound only if the cascade exists. Which order is cheaper is chosen by the formula, using the pilot's measured values.
mappings.runner: The check script at freeze and after the review; the coordinator chooses the order per wave from the pilot's numbers.
mappings.on_failure: Through the stale cascade (D2-07). The review is not accepted until no stale sentence remains.
mappings.formula: Check every pack card before the review iff (N_p - N_c)*c < p*N_c*R. Here N_p = cards in the pack, N_c = cards cited, c = checker tokens per card, p = per-card failure rate (drops and corrections separately), R = tokens to repair a citing sentence or re-review. Amendment 3's own check corrected 14 of 45 findings (p of about 0.31 for corrections, 0 drops), so cascades should be expected as routine.
mappings.fails_here: A session's window is a read set nobody tracks, and a read cannot be undone from it. Everything the researcher read can shape its review without a citation: cards later dropped, pages, the helpers' summaries. A same-window review (F1, option a) therefore reads uncommitted data by construction. A fresh reviewer working from the frozen, checked pack (option b) reads committed data only. The field's default for anything published to others is committed reads. That settles isolation, not quality: the researcher may know more. So the pilot comparison stays. Under option a, the reviewer's extra knowledge must be written down as cards, and so committed and checked, before it may be cited.

mappings.classical: Completeness of a list of failure modes, judged against a named catalogue of anomalies (relative completeness)
solutions: The catalogue of isolation anomalies: dirty write, dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, read skew, write skew [Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil, O'Neil 1995, A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, SIGMOD]
The failure catalogue of transaction processing (crash, torn write, media failure) [Gray and Reuter 1993, Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques]
mappings.rule: Keep a matrix of data against anomalies. Rows: every shared datum (question lists, cards, card_status, packs, reviews, synthesis, ledgers, journals, status file, branches). Columns: the seven anomalies, plus crash or torn write, stale derived data, and mutable identity. Each cell names a rule id or says 'accepted: reason'. Walking it now finds four risks the list lacks: write skew on cross-field coverage, non-repeatable reads of sources, a phantom in certification, and stale derived data (see missing_risks).
mappings.runner: An agent fills the matrix at each protocol amendment; a Node script refuses the amendment while any cell is empty.
mappings.on_failure: The amendment is not accepted until every cell is filled.
mappings.formula: Completeness relative to the catalogue = filled cells / (rows * columns), required to be 1.
mappings.fails_here: Faults specific to language models (confident falsehood, injection, correlated agreement) are not in these catalogues; they are Byzantine. The catalogue gives completeness for the storage and concurrency layer only, and the other fields' catalogues must cover the rest.

mappings.classical: Cost estimation and admission control from statistics, with re-planning when observed cost departs from the estimate
solutions: Cost-based plan selection from statistics [Selinger, Astrahan, Chamberlin, Lorie, Price 1979, Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System, SIGMOD]
Re-optimisation in mid-query [Kabra and DeWitt 1998, Efficient Mid-Query Re-Optimization of Sub-Optimal Query Execution Plans, SIGMOD]
mappings.rule: Estimate a field's cost per question id (t_q from the pilot, D2-01) times its questions, not as one figure per field. A wave starts iff its estimate with margin fits within the remaining cap. During the wave, the watcher compares actual spend against estimated spend for the questions covered so far, and exits for re-planning when the ratio passes a threshold. The present rule has an admission check, but its estimate is per field from one pilot, and it reacts in the run only to overspend against the allowance, not to departure from the estimate.
mappings.runner: The coordinator's admission script before each wave; the watcher during it.
mappings.on_failure: The wave is not started, or the watcher exits and the coordinator re-plans (defer, redistribute, or ask the owner).
mappings.formula: Admit iff sum over the wave's fields of (sum of t_q) * (1 + m) <= remaining cap; m is set by the owner (F4) and informed by the pilot's per-question coefficient of variation. In the run: exit when actual / (sum of t_q over the covered questions) > theta, with theta about 1.5 as a start, to be tuned.
mappings.fails_here: One pilot is a sample of one field. Costs vary between fields. Spend is visible only in transcripts, because no script can read the plan's meter. The field's answer is to estimate per unit, not per whole, and to check during the run.

mappings.classical: Injection, where data becomes code (SQL injection), and its standard fix of parameterised queries
solutions: Parameterised (prepared) statements, never escaping or filtering [Practitioner standard (OWASP guidance); I am not sure of an original paper]
mappings.rule: Treat every free-text field of a card as tainted. The card schema keeps free text to the 15-word quote and short, enumerated fields; everything else is numbers, enums and ids. The child sees cards through the render step (D2-08) as structured data. The remaining exposure is the child reading originals of must-read sources, and that must be stated as accepted, not called solved.
mappings.runner: The schema check in the commit script.
mappings.on_failure: The card is rejected and returned for re-extraction.
mappings.formula: Tainted surface = the total free-text characters per card that reach a tool-holding session; minimise it.
mappings.fails_here: A language model has one channel. No parameterisation exists, so only filtering is left, which is the approach that failed for SQL. The lesson from my field is negative: do not trust a filter. Shrink the free text that reaches a session holding tools.

missing.title: A source changes, or is read differently, between the reader and the checker
missing.classical: Non-repeatable read
missing.mechanism: Snapshot the page at card commit under its content hash, and make every later check read that snapshot (D2-09).

missing.title: Each field leaves out a shared question, assuming the neighbouring field covers it
missing.classical: Write skew on a constraint that spans several items
missing.mechanism: A script at the synthesis gate checks coverage over the union of all fields' confirmed cards against all approved question ids. A boundary question is assigned to exactly one field at plan time (D2-01).

missing.title: A dropped or corrected card survives in reviews, the synthesis and certificates
missing.classical: Stale derived data, a cascading abort that is never handled
missing.mechanism: Foreign keys with a cascade to 'stale', and a gate that refuses any artifact with stale dependencies (D2-07).

missing.title: A half-written card line or pack is read as complete after a crash, a sleep or a reboot
missing.classical: Torn write; a missing commit point
missing.mechanism: Write a temp file, rename it, then append a journal line with its hash. Recovery drops a torn tail into .corrupt (D2-03).

missing.title: A certificate or coverage figure stays in force after the set it was computed over has changed
missing.classical: Phantom (a predicate read over a set that later grows or changes)
missing.mechanism: Each certificate names the snapshot hash it was computed over, and it is void once that hash is no longer current (D2-07).

missing.title: A citation silently points at different content after a card or approach id is reused or a card is edited in place
missing.classical: Mutable identity, or key reuse, across versions
missing.mechanism: Ids are immutable. A corrected card gets a new id that points to the one it replaces, and citations carry the pack hash (copy-on-write, D2-02).

missing.title: Merged ledgers are misordered across a sleep, a reboot or two clocks
missing.classical: Ordering by physical clock in a log merge
missing.mechanism: Order by (session id, per-session sequence number); wall time is for information only (D2-05).

missing.title: The old coordinator resumes after a hand-over and writes alongside its successor
missing.classical: Lost update from two writers (in distributed systems, a stale leader without fencing)
missing.mechanism: The status file carries a coordinator epoch number. Every write script refuses an epoch lower than the current one. The hand-over increments the epoch before the successor starts.

do_not: Never discard confirmed data to make a node fit. A B+ tree never drops a key. Keep the keys and a pointer to where the rest lives (out-of-line storage), and keep every confirmed card readable by id.
Do not split a node after it has been filled at full cost, and do not split the content. Split the key range (question ids), at plan time or before the insert that would overflow.

Do not import B+ tree height or concurrency machinery (latch coupling, B-link trees) into a tree of seven leaves and three sessions. Only capacity, fill factor, key-range partitioning, never dropping a key, and copy-on-write carry over.
Do not plan recovery by re-running a brief and expecting the same result. Log values (the card or section itself), not intents.
Do not edit a frozen pack, a card or an approach id in place. Write a new version with a new hash or id, and pin every citation and certificate to the hash it read.
Do not let models retype fields a script can join (numbers, baselines, conditions). Hand-maintained copies are the update anomaly that normalisation exists to prevent.
Do not use check-then-act on a shared file. Use an atomic exclusive create or rename, or one writer.
Do not publish a derived result (review, synthesis, certificate) that read unchecked data unless a cascade exists that invalidates it when the data fails.
Do not merge logs by wall-clock time across sessions.
Do not let a hand-over note written by the coordinator stand in for a checkpoint. Derive the status from the logs by script.
Do not rely on filtering or escaping as the defence against injected text. It failed for SQL. Shrink the free-text surface instead.
Do not take passing integrity constraints as evidence of truth. They check references and scope, not whether a card is right.
result.check_overall: All 31 cited sources exist, and no citation had a wrong author, year or venue. I confirmed four by search (Yao 1978, Young 1974, Rodeh 2008, Stonebraker 1986). The rest I judged from standard records and textbook knowledge, with no fetch, so those are weaker evidence. Several claims are stretched. Yao's ln 2 (69%) is for high-order B-trees, not 2-3 trees. ARIES checkpoints are fuzzy, not complete by construction. Codd 1970 gives foreign keys but not the declared delete actions. Stonebraker's paper does not establish "no locks". The D2-whole design is the expert's own composition of components, not a source's result.

result.field: Operating systems, memory hierarchy, scheduling and cost models

whole.name: A supervision tree (Erlang/OTP) running crash-only workers, with a batch system's admission, quotas and accounting added
whole.source: Joe Armstrong, 2003, 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors' (PhD thesis, Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm). George Candea and Armando Fox, 2003, 'Crash-only software' (HotOS IX). Batch admission and accounting: Michael Litzkow, Miron Livny and Matt Mutka, 1988, 'Condor - a hunter of idle workstations' (ICDCS).
whole.borrow: (1) One supervisor per level, with a restart strategy per child: one_for_one, so one field's failure never restarts its siblings. (2) Restart intensity: at most MaxR restarts within MaxT, after which the supervisor gives up on that child and escalates to its parent. Here: a field gets at most R restarts per wave, then it is dropped with a note to the owner (D3-08). (3) Workers hold no state that cannot be rebuilt from durable files; a restart reads only committed files (D3-09). (4) Supervisors never do workers' work. (5) From batch systems: resource requests per job, admission against measured free resources, soft and hard quotas with a kill at the hard one, and a per-job accounting log, which is the ledger.

mappings.classical: Choosing the checkpoint/restart interval when holding state has a cost that grows over time: the square-root law of the economic order quantity and of the optimum checkpoint interval
solutions: Economic order quantity (square-root law) [F. W. Harris, 1913, 'How many parts to make at once', Factory, The Magazine of Management]
Optimum checkpoint interval [John W. Young, 1974, 'A first order approximation to the optimum checkpoint interval', Communications of the ACM]
mappings.rule: Hand over at a computed window size W*, not at a round 200,000. If W* comes out close to B, the task does not fit one session: split the work (D3-12) rather than hand over again.
mappings.runner: The watcher script computes W* per session from its transcript; the coordinator acts on it
mappings.on_failure: When the window passes W*, the watcher exits and the coordinator orders the hand-over. When the window passes 1.5*W*, or W* < 2*B, the coordinator stops the session and splits its remaining work.
mappings.formula: Window at call i: W_i = B + g*i. Cost of a run of k calls: k*B + g*k^2/2. Average per call: B + H/k + g*k/2. This is smallest at k* = sqrt(2H/g), so hand over when W reaches W* = B + sqrt(2*H*g). Cost version: replace g with p_cache*g and give H in cost units. The two optima differ, and the owner says which measure governs. Overall, a session's input tokens grow with the square of its length, so ceilings alone do not bound spend (P12).
mappings.fails_here: A hand-over loses information (P4), which the formula does not price. The growth rate g is not constant, since a session that reads a paper adds tokens in bursts. The reloaded state B grows with each hand-over, because the pack grows. With prompt caching, a re-read token costs less than a new one, so the optimum for token count differs from the optimum for token cost. The field's answer to a lossy restart is to put a separate bound on how many hand-overs a single task may take (see the thrashing risk) and not to fold the loss into the cost.

mappings.classical: Working set and resident-set management. The context window is a memory with no page replacement: everything loaded stays resident and is re-read on every call until the process ends.
solutions: Working set model [Peter J. Denning, 1968, 'The working set model for program behavior', Communications of the ACM]
mappings.rule: A node's window may hold only its working set: status lines and pointers for the coordinator, cards and chosen originals for a child. Anything read once (a large file, search results, a whole paper for one number) is read by a helper, which returns the extract. A node's planned intake must fit W* from D3-01, not the 1,000,000-token physical limit.
mappings.runner: The coordinator, in each child's brief. The watcher checks it.
mappings.on_failure: When a single tool result in the coordinator's window exceeds a size set from the pilot, the watcher flags it in the status file and the coordinator's next hand-over pointer excludes it.
mappings.formula: Residency efficiency = (tokens of the window that later output quotes or cites) / (window tokens). A cheap proxy is the share of tool-result tokens that come from files the session later cites. Each loaded token costs about (calls remaining) * p_cache, so load a T-token item through a helper whenever T * calls_remaining * p_cache > the helper's own cost.
mappings.fails_here: A window offers no per-page eviction. The only ways to evict are to end the session or to compact it, which is lossy, so the resident set is everything loaded so far. When paging is impossible, the field's answer is to keep large objects out of resident memory in the first place: hold a reference and fetch on demand. Here a helper does the fetch: its own window absorbs the large read and only a compact result comes back.

mappings.classical: Thrashing, and load control of the degree of multiprogramming
solutions: Load control by working set (admit a process only if its working set fits; deactivate one when memory runs short) [Peter J. Denning, 1968, 'Thrashing: its causes and prevention', AFIPS Fall Joint Computer Conference]
mappings.rule: Admit a new session only if os.freemem() - reserve >= the peak resident size of a session as measured in the pilot. If free memory falls below the reserve during a wave, stop the newest session; it restarts from its checkpoint.
mappings.runner: A launcher check in the watcher script (Node: os.freemem; per-process size via the built-in tasklist command)
mappings.on_failure: The session is not started and the wave waits. When memory is low mid-wave, the watcher exits with 'memory' and the coordinator stops the newest session.
mappings.formula: admit iff free - reserve >= max_RSS_session. Keep the cap of three as an upper bound only.
mappings.fails_here: The PC's memory is also taken by things outside the tree: WSL, Docker and emulators. The owner's own records show 46 hard resets attributed to over-commit. A fixed count of three sessions is a static multiprogramming level, and it is wrong whenever other load changes.

mappings.classical: Admission control under uncertain job sizes: predicting the next burst from past ones
solutions: Exponential averaging of measured job lengths (the standard estimator for shortest-job-first scheduling) [Abraham Silberschatz, Peter B. Galvin, Greg Gagne, 2018, 'Operating System Concepts' (10th ed.), CPU scheduling chapter]
mappings.rule: A wave starts only if sum over its fields of est_f * (1 + m) <= R. The estimate is updated after every field that ends, and the margin m is the largest overrun seen so far, never less than the owner's floor.
mappings.runner: The coordinator (it alone can read the meter), using a script that computes est_f and m from the merged ledger
mappings.on_failure: Do not start the wave. Run a smaller wave in the order of D3-14, or stop and report.
mappings.formula: est_{n+1} = a*t_n + (1-a)*est_n, with a = 0.5 to start. m = max over finished fields of (t_f / est_f_at_admission - 1), floored at the owner's margin. Keep a separate estimate per field class if classes differ.
mappings.fails_here: The pilot is a single sample, and it comes from the measurement field, which may differ from the others. Only a session can read the usage meter, so admission needs a session's turn. The field's standard response to a high-variance estimate is to admit on a pessimistic estimate (the largest overrun observed) and to enforce a per-job quota at run time (D3-05), so a bad estimate cannot overspend.

mappings.classical: Resource quotas with soft and hard limits (rlimit) enforced from outside the process
solutions: Soft and hard resource limits (getrlimit/setrlimit: a signal at the soft limit, termination at the hard one) [IEEE Std 1003.1 (POSIX), getrlimit/setrlimit]
mappings.rule: Each child has an allowance A_f. At the soft limit 0.8*A_f, the child is told to freeze: write its cards and pack, which is write-back (D3-13). At the hard limit A_f - overshoot, it is stopped.
mappings.runner: The watcher counts from the transcripts; the coordinator stops the session
mappings.on_failure: Watcher exit 'overspend'. The coordinator stops the session and marks the field 'cut at quota', with its frozen files kept.
mappings.formula: hard = A_f - (poll_interval + wake_latency) * peak_spend_rate. soft = 0.8 * A_f.
mappings.fails_here: The kernel enforces at once. Here the count comes from the transcript a poll later, and only the coordinator can stop a session, so a stop waits for its wake. The overshoot is therefore poll interval plus wake latency, times the spend rate, and the hard limit must sit that much below the true allowance.

mappings.classical: The watchdog timer, and telling livelock from progress
solutions: A progress-kicked watchdog: the dog is kicked from the point where work completes, never from a separate liveness timer [Standard embedded and OS practice; I know of no single original paper]
mappings.rule: Progress means a new confirmed card id, or a new output file whose content hash has not been seen. A rewrite to an old hash does not count. A loop is k identical tool-call signatures in a row in the transcript. Suspend is a gap between polls greater than the interval plus slack; it extends all deadlines by the gap and is logged.
mappings.runner: The watcher script
mappings.on_failure: Exit 'no progress' or 'loop', which wakes the coordinator. It stops the session before a replacement starts, as in P9's current rule. Suspend does not cause an exit, only a log line.
mappings.formula: Time box T = the 95th percentile of intervals between progress events in the pilot, times 2. Loop: signature(call_i) = hash(tool name + arguments), repeated k=3 times.
mappings.fails_here: Sleep and hibernation stop the watcher too, so on resume the wall clock jumps and every time box expires at once (a false stall, then a mass kill). A session can produce files without progress, for example by rewriting the same file. The field's answer to the clock jump is to detect suspend as a gap between polls and to shift every deadline by that gap.

mappings.classical: Lost wakeup, and level-triggered versus edge-triggered notification (a notify is a hint); interrupt coalescing
solutions: Mesa monitor semantics: a notify is only a hint, so the woken party re-checks the condition in a loop [Butler W. Lampson and David D. Redell, 1980, 'Experience with processes and monitors in Mesa', Communications of the ACM]
mappings.rule: The watcher appends every event to the status file before it exits. The coordinator, on every wake, reads the whole status file and not just the exit reason. Before ending its turn, the coordinator starts a new watcher, whose first act is to evaluate every condition. For non-urgent events (done, repair request), the watcher waits up to delta after the first one, to gather others, before it exits. Urgent events (overspend, memory, stall) exit at once.
mappings.runner: The watcher script and the coordinator
mappings.on_failure: If the coordinator ends a turn with no watcher running, nobody notices. To prevent that, every turn ends with a check that a watcher process is alive, and its pid is written to the status file.
mappings.formula: Cost of waking = wakes * W_coord * p_cache. Choose delta so that the expected extra delay is below the time box divided by 10.
mappings.fails_here: The watcher exits on the first event. Events that happen while the coordinator is mid-turn, or between the exit and the next watcher's start, have nobody watching for them. Each wake also costs at least one read of the coordinator's whole window, so wakes are expensive interrupts and should be coalesced.

mappings.classical: Restart storms, and restart intensity in supervision
solutions: Supervisor restart intensity (MaxR restarts within MaxT, then give up and escalate) [Joe Armstrong, 2003, 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors' (PhD thesis, Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm)]
mappings.rule: A field may restart at most twice per wave. The second restart must change its input: a narrower question range, a repaired pack, or another model where the owner allows one. A third failure drops the field with a note to the owner.
mappings.runner: The coordinator, from a restart counter that the watcher keeps in the status file
mappings.on_failure: The field is dropped and listed as 'not covered', and the refuter of P15 sees that drop.
mappings.formula: MaxR = 2 per field per wave. Escalate on MaxR + 1.
mappings.fails_here: A fault that comes from the brief or the pack is systematic, and because sessions of one model fail alike (P3), a replacement repeats it. A restart is also expensive.

mappings.classical: Checkpoint/restart with atomic commit: recovering from durable state in a system that is not deterministic
solutions: A commit record written last (write-ahead and atomic replace) [Jim Gray and Andreas Reuter, 1993, 'Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques']
Optimum checkpoint interval [John W. Young, 1974, 'A first order approximation to the optimum checkpoint interval', Communications of the ACM]
mappings.rule: Every file a session produces is written to name.tmp and then renamed into place (same volume). A per-folder manifest of (path, sha256) is updated last, and it is the commit record. The restart path reads only what the manifest lists. A card is committed as soon as it is made, so a crash loses at most the in-window understanding not yet written down.
mappings.runner: A tiny Node write helper used by the child, and the restart script
mappings.on_failure: An unlisted or mismatched file is ignored on restart and logged. Anything downstream of a regenerated file is marked for a new check.
mappings.formula: Expected loss per crash = lambda * (unwritten in-window work). lambda is measurable from the Windows event log (unexpected-shutdown events): the owner's record is 46 hard resets in about 60 days, so M is about 1.3 days, and Young gives T_opt = sqrt(2*C*M). With C at one card's write, write each card immediately.
mappings.fails_here: Log-replay recovery assumes the process is piecewise deterministic. Sessions are not, so re-running a lost step gives different text. The field's answer is to recover only from committed outputs, never by replay, and to treat a regenerated file as new data that must be checked again.

mappings.classical: TOCTOU (a race between time of check and time of use) on a shared claim, and its standard fix by atomic test-and-set; leases for holders that crash
