solutions: Atomic exclusive create as the lock primitive (O_CREAT|O_EXCL; in Node fs.openSync(path,'wx'); on NTFS CREATE_NEW) [Matt Bishop and Michael Dilger, 1996, 'Checking for race conditions in file accesses', Computing Systems]
Leases [Cary G. Gray and David R. Cheriton, 1989, 'Leases: an efficient fault-tolerant mechanism for distributed file cache consistency', SOSP]
mappings.rule: One file per source, at claims/<sha256 of the normalised DOI or URL>, created with 'wx' and holding the field, session and start time. It lives outside every worktree. If the file already exists, the child waits for the claimant's card and reads it (read-only) instead of sending a reader. If it needs a different aspect of the source, it reads the source anyway and logs a duplicate. A claim older than the lease with no card is stale: it is taken over by atomic rename.
mappings.runner: A claim script that the child runs before giving a source to a reader
mappings.on_failure: Contention or a script error means read anyway and log it. A claim never blocks work.
mappings.formula: Lease = the 95th percentile of read-to-card time in the pilot, times 2.
mappings.fails_here: None of the primitive's assumptions fails. One PC and one NTFS volume meet them. The register was withdrawn because of a race that the standard primitive removes. Its other objection, that a claim blocks a neighbouring field, is a policy choice: make the claim a shared-cache entry, not an exclusive lock on reading. Readers have no write tools, so the child makes the claim.

mappings.classical: Speed-up laws: a serial fraction, plus coherence costs that grow with the number of workers
solutions: Amdahl's law [Gene M. Amdahl, 1967, 'Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities', AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference]
Universal Scalability Law [Neil J. Gunther, 2007, 'Guerrilla Capacity Planning', Springer]
mappings.rule: Report the tree's result as two numbers: wall-time speed-up against the single-session control, and the work ratio (tree tokens divided by single-session tokens). Fit s from the ledger before raising concurrency.
mappings.runner: A ledger script after the pilot and after each wave
mappings.on_failure: If the measured S(3) is below S(2) plus a noise allowance, run waves of 2.
mappings.formula: s = (wall time with no child running) / total wall time. S(N) <= 1/(s + (1-s)/N). USL: X(N) = X1*N/(1 + alpha*(N-1) + beta*N*(N-1)), with N* = sqrt((1-alpha)/beta).
mappings.fails_here: These laws are about time, not tokens: parallel children never lower total token count, they add the coordinator's overhead. The serial part here includes the owner's approvals and the coordinator's gates. With N at most 3 the fit has three points, so it gives a reading, not a law.

mappings.classical: Choosing the fan-out under a cost that grows with the square of resident size: superlinear gains from splitting a job into pieces that each fit the economic memory size
solutions: The cost model of D3-01 applied to partitioning (the same reason cache-sized blocking beats one large working set) [Derived here from the cost structure; the square-root law is Harris 1913 and Young 1974. No single source for the partitioning step.]
mappings.rule: Before the pilot, predict the single-session control's tokens and the tree's tokens from measured g, n and H. The P18 comparison then tests a stated prediction. Fields are not split mid-research. A planned field whose predicted window exceeds W* gets a second session that runs after it, from its frozen pack (a hand-over), and is not cut in two.
mappings.runner: The coordinator, from a planning script
mappings.on_failure: If the prediction is off by more than a factor of 2, the cost model is wrong. Re-measure g and stop trusting the fan-out choice.
mappings.formula: Single session: T1 = n*B + g*n^2/2. Tree with k equal leaves: Tk = n*B + g*n^2/(2k) + k*H + Coord(k), where Coord(k) is about m*B_c + g_c*m^2/2 and g_c is roughly proportional to k*s. The tree wins on tokens when g*n^2*(1 - 1/k)/2 > k*H + Coord(k). Ignoring Coord, k_opt = n*sqrt(g/(2H)).
mappings.fails_here: Fields are not equal parts. Splitting cuts knowledge apart (the withdrawn split rule), which this model does not price. The coordinator's cost grows with k.

mappings.classical: Write-back caching (dirty data is lost at eviction unless flushed), plus crash-only design (exercise the recovery path)
solutions: Flush dirty lines before eviction (write-back with a flush) [Alan Jay Smith, 1982, 'Cache memories', ACM Computing Surveys]
Crash-only software [George Candea and Armando Fox, 2003, 'Crash-only software', HotOS IX]
mappings.rule: Before any review, the child flushes: everything it intends to rely on becomes a confirmed card or a pack line. The review then runs in a fresh session from the frozen pack, which is the same path a crash or a full window takes. F1's pilot comparison remains the test of what is lost.
mappings.runner: The child (flush), the watcher (it checks the freeze hash), and the coordinator (starts the reviewer)
mappings.on_failure: With no frozen pack hash there is no review. If the fresh review scores below the same-window review on the pre-fixed score by more than the owner's tolerance, use same-window reviews.
mappings.formula: Extra cost of a same-window review = n_r * (W_research - B_pack) * p_cache, where n_r is the number of review calls.
mappings.fails_here: The researcher's dirty state includes impressions it cannot state as cards, and those cannot be flushed. But the review may cite only cards (P1, P17), so that unflushed state is uncitable by rule. It can enter a same-window review only as uncited bias. The cost side is direct: each review call in the researcher's window re-reads W_research instead of B_pack.

mappings.classical: Single-machine scheduling to minimise weighted completion time, under a budget that may be cut
solutions: Smith's rule (weighted shortest processing time: order by w/p, highest first) [W. E. Smith, 1956, 'Various optimizers for single-stage production', Naval Research Logistics Quarterly]
mappings.rule: Respect the precedence constraints first (pilot, then the rest). Within a wave, start fields in descending order of owner weight divided by estimated cost.
mappings.runner: The coordinator
mappings.on_failure: If the owner gives no weights, all are equal and the cheapest goes first. Aging: a field passed over twice gets its weight doubled, so it does not starve.
mappings.formula: priority_f = w_f / est_f. Aging: w_f *= 2 after each wave in which f was admissible but not run.
mappings.fails_here: There are precedence constraints: the measurement field defines the scoring, and the pilot provides the cost estimates. Costs are estimates (D3-04).

missing.title: Deadlock on the session slots
missing.classical: Deadlock: hold and wait over a counted resource (Coffman, Elphick, Shoshani, 1971, 'System deadlocks', ACM Computing Surveys)
missing.mechanism: Break hold and wait: a child that asks for a repair commits its files and ends, which frees its slot, and restarts from its checkpoint later. Alternatively, always keep one slot reserved for the coordinator's repairs. The watcher counts sessions that are waiting and holding a slot.

missing.title: Lost wakeups between the watcher's exit and its restart
missing.classical: Lost-wakeup problem (Mesa semantics, Lampson and Redell 1980)
missing.mechanism: D3-07: a level-triggered status file, a watcher whose first act is to check every condition, and a check at the end of every turn that a watcher is alive.

missing.title: Hand-over thrashing
missing.classical: Thrashing (Denning 1968): fault-service time dominates useful work
missing.mechanism: The watcher computes overhead = (reload + hand-over tokens) / total tokens per task. When the useful tokens between hand-overs fall below the reload cost B, stop handing over and split the work (D3-01, D3-12).

missing.title: Sleep or resume triggers false timeouts, then a burst of simultaneous restarts
missing.classical: Clock discontinuity on suspend; thundering herd
missing.mechanism: D3-06: detect suspend from the gap between polls and shift deadlines. Stagger restarts, one at a time, each admitted by D3-03.

missing.title: Orphaned process trees and leaked resources after a stop
missing.classical: Orphan processes and resource leaks on termination
missing.mechanism: Stop the whole process tree (Windows taskkill /T, or a job object), then verify by the session's process list and the container and volume counts before admitting a replacement. The watcher logs any leftovers.

missing.title: The coordinator is a single serial server, and queueing at it grows sharply
missing.classical: Queueing at a bottleneck server (utilisation near 1; Little's law)
missing.mechanism: Measure rho from the ledger (the coordinator's busy time over wall time). Keep rho low with gate scripts in place of reading (P11), coalesced wakes (D3-07), and smaller waves when rho exceeds 0.7.

missing.title: A large field starves under admission
missing.classical: Starvation (fixed by aging)
missing.mechanism: Aging in D3-14, plus an explicit 'never admitted' line that the owner sees.

missing.title: A crash loop burns the allowance
missing.classical: Restart storm (supervisor restart intensity)
missing.mechanism: D3-08: MaxR = 2 per field per wave, the second restart must change its input, then escalate to the owner.

missing.title: After a reboot nothing resumes and nobody notices
missing.classical: No init or supervisor on boot
missing.mechanism: Recovery only through the owner's next session: its first act reads the status file, and the restart path rebuilds from it. Optionally, a logon-triggered Windows scheduled task tells the owner (the owner's decision). Whether any watcher can keep the PC awake remains not established.

do_not: Do not set the hand-over point as a round number (200,000 or 300,000). Compute W* from measured g, B and H, and compute it separately for token count and for token cost.
Do not treat a window ceiling as a spend bound. Spend grows with the square of a session's length, so enforce per-session quotas with a soft and a hard limit.
Do not use liveness (a heartbeat, an open process) as progress. Kick the watchdog only on new confirmed output.
Do not measure time boxes in wall time without detecting suspend.
Do not recover by replaying a step and expecting the same output. Sessions are not deterministic, so recover only from committed files and check anything regenerated again.
Do not implement any claim or lock as check-then-write on a shared file. Use atomic exclusive create or rename, with a lease.
Do not fix the number of concurrent sessions while other load on the PC varies. Admit against measured free memory.
Do not add concurrency past the measured knee. Parallel children never lower token count; they lower time only up to the serial fraction.
Do not restart without a limit, and do not restart with an unchanged input after a repeated failure.
Do not let a child hold a session slot while it waits on the coordinator.
Do not stop a session without stopping its process tree and checking for leaked processes, containers and volumes.
Do not wake the coordinator on every small event. Each wake re-reads its whole window, so coalesce the events that are not urgent.
Do not write a file in place where a crash can leave half of it. Write to a temporary name, rename, then update the manifest last.

sources_with_a_problem.source: Standard embedded and OS practice; no single paper
sources_with_a_problem.note: No source is cited, so there is nothing to check. Progress-kicked watchdogs are common practice but the claimed detection bound was not verified against any reference.

result.check_overall: All cited sources exist with correct authors, years and venues. Search records confirmed Young 1974, Bishop and Dilger 1996 and Condor 1988. The rest were checked against my own knowledge of the standard record, not by opening them. Claims are weak in four places. (1) Condor 1988 does not describe declared resources, admission, quotas or accounting. (2) POSIX rlimit has no uniform signal-at-soft-limit rule and no overrun bound. (3) Bishop and Dilger is about TOCTTOU detection, not the exclusive-create lock guarantee. (4) The Amdahl closed form and the MaxR/MaxT parameters are later formalisations, not printed in the cited works. D3-06 cites no source, and D3-12 says openly that it has none. No page text asked me to do anything.

whole.name: An assurance case (claim, argument, evidence) built under independent verification and validation, run on a supervision tree. The assurance case covers value faults: false, distorted or misapplied claims. The supervision tree covers crash faults: stall, crash, loop, reboot.
whole.source: Kelly, T.P. (1998), 'Arguing Safety: A Systematic Approach to Managing Safety Cases', PhD thesis, University of York (Goal Structuring Notation, GSN). IEEE Std 1012, 'Standard for System, Software, and Hardware Verification and Validation'. Armstrong, J. (2003), 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors', PhD thesis, KTH (Erlang/OTP supervision trees).
whole.borrow: From GSN: the element types (goal, strategy, solution, context, assumption, justification, undeveloped) and a mechanical trace from every claim to its evidence. A required counter-evidence (defeater) node on each top claim. From IEEE 1012: the three kinds of independence (technical, managerial, financial), and the rule that the V&V plan is fixed before the work starts. That plan includes every checker brief and every gate threshold. From OTP: the one_for_one restart strategy; a restart intensity (at most MaxR restarts within MaxT, then escalate to the parent); supervisors that hold only pointers and status; workers that hold the state.

mappings.classical: Measuring how well a checker detects faults: its coverage, or diagnostic coverage. A detector whose rate was never measured reports 'nothing found', and that cannot be told apart from 'nothing there'. The tree has six checkers: the card checker, the citation check after the review, the quote script, the refuter, external certification, and the schema script. None of them has a measured detection rate.
solutions: Error seeding [Mills, H.D. (1972), 'On the Statistical Validation of Computer Programs', IBM Federal Systems Division report FSC-72-6015]
Mutation analysis [DeMillo, R.A., Lipton, R.J., Sayward, F.G. (1978), 'Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer', IEEE Computer 11(4)]

Fault injection to validate error-detection mechanisms [Arlat, J., Aguera, M., Amat, L., Crouzet, Y., Fabre, J.-C., Laprie, J.-C., Martins, E., Powell, D. (1990), 'Fault Injection for Dependability Validation: A Methodology and Some Applications', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. 16(2)]
mappings.rule: No checker is trusted until its detection rate has been measured for each fault class on blind seeded items. After that, every check batch carries a small seed as a proof test.
mappings.runner: A Node script seed.js makes the mutants with deterministic operators applied to confirmed cards and to frozen copies of reviews. It writes the key to a folder that only the coordinator can read. A second script, score-seeds.js, scores the results. The coordinator starts both scripts. The checker sessions run with their fixed brief, which does not change and does not mention seeding.
mappings.on_failure: If the lower 95 % bound of a class's detection rate is below the threshold the owner set in advance, the next wave does not start. The check is changed (its prompt, its batch size, or its model under F3) and measured again. Items that this checker 'confirmed' in that class are relabelled 'checked by an unqualified checker'.
mappings.formula: Per fault class k: detection d_k = s_k / S_k, with a Clopper-Pearson interval (Clopper, C.J. & Pearson, E.S. (1934), Biometrika 26). Estimated real faults N_k = n_k * S_k / s_k, so the residual is N_k - n_k. Mutation score = killed / (mutants - equivalent mutants). Seeds needed to show d_k >= d0 at 95 % confidence with zero misses: S_k >= ln(0.05) / ln(d0). That is about 29 for d0 = 0.9 and 14 for d0 = 0.8. With zero misses in S items, the 95 % upper bound on the miss rate is about 3/S.
mappings.fails_here: Representativeness. Nobody knows how a model's own fabrications are distributed. Mutants written by hand may be easier to catch than real errors, for example a number that is plainly out of place, or harder. If the same model generates the mutants, they share the checker's blind spots. A checker may recognise the style of the seeding. Outputs are not reproducible, so the detection rate is a distribution over runs, not one number. When representativeness fails, the field does three things. It builds mutation operators from the failure classes actually observed. It re-injects real defects found earlier ('defect reinjection'). It reports coverage per class, with confidence bounds, never as one pooled figure.

mappings.classical: Common-mode (coincident) failure in design diversity, as in N-version programming and duplex comparison. Independently built versions fail together on the same inputs, so their agreement is weaker evidence than independence would predict.
solutions: N-version programming [Avizienis, A. (1985), 'The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-11(12)]
Coincident-failure model [Eckhardt, D.E. & Lee, L.D. (1985), 'A Theoretical Basis for the Analysis of Multiversion Software Subject to Coincident Errors', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-11(12)]
Experimental test of independence [Knight, J.C. & Leveson, N.G. (1986), 'An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-12(1)]
Forced diversity [Littlewood, B. & Miller, D.R. (1989), 'Conceptual Modeling of Coincident Failures in Multiversion Software', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. 15(12)]

Consensus recovery block (comparison, then adjudication by an acceptance test) [Scott, R.K., Gault, J.W., McAllister, D.F. (1987), 'Fault-Tolerant Software Reliability Modeling', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-13(5)]
mappings.rule: P3's rule ('agreement never raises a claim; a disagreement marks it weak, and adjudication is by checking the source') is standard: it is duplex comparison with adjudication by an acceptance test. What is missing is the rule for P20 and F2. A second opinion is admitted only along an axis where the measured beta is below a threshold the owner sets.
mappings.runner: The seeding scripts of D4-01, run in the pilot on the same seeded set by every candidate second opinion: the same model reviewing the same pack; a different model, if F3 allows one; the same model with a different perspective brief. The coordinator reads the score file.
mappings.on_failure: If beta is at or above the threshold (for example 0.7), that second opinion is not run in later waves, which also saves its spend. If no diverse option exists, the synthesis says 'no independent second opinion' rather than appearing to have one. Decide F2 by where the residual faults sit. If they are mostly faults in the pack (wrong selection of cards, missing contrary evidence), a second reviewer of the same pack cannot catch them; use the contrary reader or a second research run. If they are mostly reviewer faults (misused cards, wrong verdicts), use a second reviewer with a forced-diverse brief or model.
mappings.formula: From the seeded items: p_A = miss rate of A, p_B = miss rate of B, p_AB = joint miss rate. Independence ratio r = p_AB / (p_A * p_B), where r = 1 means independent. Beta factor = p_AB / min(p_A, p_B), the beta-factor model of common-cause failure (Fleming, K.N. (1974), General Atomic report GA-A13284). Detection added by B = p_A - p_AB. Eckhardt-Lee: P(A and B both fail on input X) = (E theta)^2 + Var(theta).
mappings.fails_here: Two instances of one model share one difficulty function theta(x), so the beta factor for their systematic errors is close to 1. Runs are not reproducible, so they show apparent diversity: a disagreement may be sampling noise and not a real detection, while agreement on a systematic error looks like confirmation. With N = 2 there is no majority, so a pair can detect a fault but cannot correct it. A second reviewer of the same frozen pack shares the pack as a common specification. That is the source of common faults that Knight and Leveson found, so it cannot see faults in the pack. When independence fails, the field: (a) uses comparison only to detect faults, never to vote; (b) sends every disagreement to an acceptance test, here the source-tied check; (c) forces diversity along the axis of the error, by a different model (F3), a different method (a perspective-based brief, or the contrary-evidence reader), or different inputs; (d) measures the coupling directly and does not assume it.

mappings.classical: Where to put the correctness check in a chain of hand-overs: the end-to-end argument.
solutions: End-to-end argument [Saltzer, J.H., Reed, D.P., Clark, D.D. (1984), 'End-to-End Arguments in System Design', ACM Trans. Computer Systems 2(4)]
mappings.rule: Every factual sentence in every review and in the synthesis is checked end to end by a script along the chain: sentence, card id, card fields, snapshot bytes. Typed hand-overs (P4) stay, as the per-hop performance measure. The P21 script must check the number and the condition fields as well as the quote. A quote match alone shows only that the passage exists.
mappings.runner: snapshot.js, run by the child when a card is taken in (D4-04), fetches the page itself and stores its raw bytes, sha256 and fetch date in the field folder; the card records the hash. e2e-check.js is run by the coordinator after each review and again after the synthesis.
mappings.on_failure: The result is three-valued: pass, fail, or not-run. A failed sentence is removed from the synthesis or marked 'unchecked'. A not-run sentence is labelled 'unverifiable' and counted, never passed. If a field's failure rate is above the threshold set in advance, its review goes back for repair.
mappings.formula: The snapshot hash must equal the hash on the card. Normalise the snapshot text with NFKC, case folding, whitespace collapse and de-hyphenation, then search for the quote. Find the card's number in the text and report its distance from the quote. Then check: sentence.number == card.number and sentence.conditions == card.conditions, field by field, which should be exact because the fields were copied. Report the share of sentences that pass, fail and are unverifiable. Per hop, report which condition field was dropped and where.
mappings.fails_here: The real endpoint is the owner, who cannot reopen every source. The source text reaches an agent through a small model's summary. Pages change, are rendered by script, are PDFs, or are behind a paywall. Only plain Node is available: zlib is built in, but PDF text extraction is crude. So the check moves to the last automated point that holds the original bytes. Those bytes are snapshotted and hashed when the card is taken in. What cannot be checked is labelled 'unverifiable', never passed (fail-safe default).

mappings.classical: Containing defects within the phase that made them: inspect at each phase exit, because a defect found later costs more and has already been built on.
solutions: Design and code inspections with entry and exit criteria, recorded defects, rework and follow-up [Fagan, M.E. (1976), 'Design and Code Inspections to Reduce Errors in Program Development', IBM Systems Journal 15(3)]
Cost of a defect rises with the phase that finds it [Boehm, B.W. (1981), 'Software Engineering Economics', Prentice-Hall]
mappings.rule: Two checks. At card intake, the script part of D4-03 runs: quote and number found in the snapshot. A failed card is quarantined in quarantine.jsonl and never enters the pack. Exit criterion for gate A: every card in the pack passed the script or is labelled unverifiable. After the review, the model's judgment check runs on the cited cards (number, conditions, whether the citing sentence stays within them), as now.
mappings.runner: intake.js, run by the child after each batch from a reader. The watcher counts cards that passed the script as progress (D4-06). The coordinator applies the exit criterion at gate A.
mappings.on_failure: The card is quarantined. If a reader's quarantine rate is above the threshold, that reader's whole batch is read again by a fresh reader.
mappings.formula: Phase containment effectiveness = defects found at intake / (defects found at intake + defects of that kind found later, including seeded defects that escaped).
mappings.fails_here: Amendment 3 moved the only card check to after the review, because 'no conclusion exists yet' earlier. But an unconfirmed false card sits in the expert's window while it reasons. It can shape judgment sentences that cite nothing, and the citation check never catches those. A defect found after the review means the review has to be redone. The field's answer is to put a cheap check at intake and keep the expensive judgment check where the conclusion exists.

mappings.classical: Completeness of a hazard analysis: deriving a list of failure modes by a systematic method instead of judgment, and estimating what that list still misses.
solutions: STPA (System-Theoretic Process Analysis) [Leveson, N.G. (2011), 'Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety', MIT Press]
FMEA [MIL-STD-1629A (1980), 'Procedures for Performing a Failure Mode, Effects and Criticality Analysis']
Fault tree analysis [Vesely, W.E., Goldberg, F.F., Roberts, N.H., Haasl, D.F. (1981), 'Fault Tree Handbook', NUREG-0492, US Nuclear Regulatory Commission]

Taxonomy of failure modes (guide words) [Avizienis, A., Laprie, J.-C., Randell, B., Landwehr, C. (2004), 'Basic Concepts and Taxonomy of Dependable and Secure Computing', IEEE Trans. Dependable and Secure Computing 1(1)]

Capture-recapture estimate of defects missed by inspectors [Eick, S.G., Loader, C.R., Long, M.D., Votta, L.G., Vander Wiel, S. (1992), 'Estimating Software Fault Content Before Coding', Proc. ICSE 14]
mappings.rule: The problem list is derived, not brainstormed. (a) STPA. Draw the control structure: owner, coordinator, watcher, children, helpers, checkers, scripts, git, the OS and its power state, the usage meter. Mark the control actions (start, brief, stop, admit a wave, repair, freeze, accept) and the feedback (notes, status files, watcher exits, ledger). For every action, write one row for each of the four unsafe types: not provided; provided when unsafe; too early, too late or out of order; stopped too soon or applied too long. Mark process-model flaws, such as a coordinator believing a stale status file. (b) FMEA. Cross every component with the Avizienis et al. modes plus the language-model modes. (c) Map P1 to P21 onto the rows. A row with no P-id is a candidate missing risk; a P-id with no row shows a gap in the model. (d) Capture-recapture between the STPA list and the FMEA list. (e) Operational feedback (FRACAS: failure reporting, analysis and corrective action): every failure in the ledger is classified to a row.
mappings.runner: A leaf session, not the coordinator, writes the tables as JSON. A Node script checks that every cell is filled or marked 'not applicable' with a reason, does the mapping, and computes the estimate.
mappings.on_failure: If the pilot has a high-severity failure that maps to no row, or the residual estimate is above the owner's threshold, waves do not start until the analysis is redone.
mappings.formula: Chapman estimator: N = (n1 + 1)(n2 + 1) / (m + 1) - 1, where n1 = items in the STPA list, n2 = items in the FMEA list, m = items in both. Residual = N - (n1 + n2 - m). STPA table rows = control actions x 4. FRACAS escape rate = failures in the ledger that map to no row / all failures in the ledger.
mappings.fails_here: Two same-model analysts are not independent, so the capture-recapture estimate is biased low. The fix is diversity of method: STPA against FMEA, not two runs of one method. The control-structure model would be drawn by the coordinator, the party under analysis. Failure-mode libraries made for hardware lack the language-model modes: fabrication, following injected text, agreeing with the brief. These are added as guide words. No method proves completeness. The field claims a method, its model, an estimate of the residual, and feedback from operation.

mappings.classical: Watchdog supervision of execution: supervision of being alive, of deadlines, and of logical (program-flow) order. The watchdog must be independent of what it supervises.
solutions: Watchdog with a separate time base; time-window watchdog; combined temporal and logical monitoring of program sequence [IEC 61508-7:2010, Annex A (techniques and measures for controlling failures)]
Alive, deadline and logical supervision [AUTOSAR Classic Platform, Specification of Watchdog Manager (version not cited)]
mappings.rule: Three kinds of supervision for each child. Alive: the transcript file keeps growing. Deadline: each stage checkpoint is reached within its time box. Logical: checkpoints arrive in order: a new question id is covered by a card that passed the script (D4-04), then the pack is frozen, then the review is written. A loop is a repetition of tool-call signatures, or no new question id covered within K cards. The watcher checks itself: on every tick it compares the gap in wall-clock time with the gap in monotonic time (process.hrtime). A gap more than twice the tick means the PC slept, and the watcher exits with the reason 'slept'. It writes its own heartbeat file, and the coordinator checks that file's age on every turn.
mappings.runner: A Node watcher started by the coordinator in the background for each wave. Its exit wakes the coordinator.
mappings.on_failure: The exit reason goes to the coordinator. It stops the stalled session first (fail-stop), then restarts the child under D4-07 or drops the field with a note.
mappings.formula: progress = new distinct question ids covered by cards that passed the script, per unit time. A stall is progress of 0 over T_box. A loop is a Jaccard similarity above J between the last k tool-call signatures (tool name plus hashed arguments). Sleep is detected when (wall-clock delta - monotonic delta) is greater than the tick.
mappings.fails_here: The watcher runs on the same PC, so sleep and reboot stop both the watcher and the watched: a common mode. Progress for a model is semantic, and a looping session can write new files (padding), so a count of files can be gamed. There is also a contradiction inside the protocol. The progress measure is 'new confirmed cards', but under P1's current rule confirmation happens only after the review, so during Stage A this measure cannot move. The field's answer: define checkpoints that can be checked mechanically; give the watcher a self-check; have someone watch the watcher.

mappings.classical: Backward error recovery: restarting from a consistent recovery point, with a limit on restarts and escalation of faults that repeat deterministically.
solutions: Recovery points and backward error recovery (and the domino effect) [Randell, B. (1975), 'System Structure for Software Fault Tolerance', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-1(2)]
Supervision trees with a restart intensity [Armstrong, J. (2003), 'Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors', PhD thesis, KTH]
Restart cures transient faults (Heisenbugs) but not deterministic ones (Bohrbugs) [Gray, J. (1985), 'Why Do Computers Stop and What Can Be Done About It?', Tandem Technical Report 85.7]
mappings.rule: (1) Every state file is written to a temporary file and then renamed. On restore, a JSONL file is validated line by line and a torn last line is dropped. (2) The restore is validated before any replacement starts. The pack hash must equal the frozen record, and the cards must be schema-valid and agree with the pack. (3) At most 1 restart per field per stage. A second failure at the same stage escalates to the owner, or the field is dropped with a note. (4) The reason for each restart is recorded. If the same failure class recurs, the brief or pack is repaired before any further session starts.
mappings.runner: The coordinator runs restore-check.js before it starts the replacement. The restart counter is kept in the coordinator's status file.
mappings.on_failure: If the pack is invalid, restore from cards.jsonl. If the cards are invalid too, the field is dropped and the owner is told.
mappings.formula: MaxR = 1 per stage. Spend wasted on restarts is at most (MaxR + 1) x the cost of a stage.
mappings.fails_here: A restart here is expensive. A fault rooted in the brief or the pack recurs on restart: it is a Bohrbug. State that was never written down is lost by definition. An append to cards.jsonl can be torn by a crash. pack.md and cards.jsonl can disagree with each other. The field's answer: atomic writes; validate the checkpoint before restoring; a restart intensity of 1; a fault that recurs is treated as deterministic, so the input is changed, not just the session.

mappings.classical: Recovery block: a primary, an acceptance test, and an alternate that runs from saved state. The alternate path is exercised only rarely.
solutions: Recovery blocks [Randell, B. (1975), 'System Structure for Software Fault Tolerance', IEEE Trans. Software Eng. SE-1(2)]
End-to-end argument (state that was never recorded cannot be checked) [Saltzer, J.H., Reed, D.P., Clark, D.D. (1984), 'End-to-End Arguments in System Design', ACM Trans. Computer Systems 2(4)]
mappings.rule: The pilot writes both reviews, as amendment 3 recommends. They are adjudicated blind by the same acceptance test: the end-to-end check of D4-03, the judgment check of conditions, and the planted defects of D4-11. Whichever form is chosen, the fresh-from-pack path runs at least once per wave, so that the alternate stays tested.
mappings.runner: The coordinator starts both reviews in the pilot. Scripts score them.
mappings.on_failure: The owner chooses from the scores. If the alternate fails in a wave where it was exercised, the restart path of D4-07 is marked unsafe until it is repaired.
mappings.formula: For each review: e2e failure rate; rate of use outside conditions; plants found out of k; share of sentences labelled judgment (an output of the same-session review that cannot be checked); tokens.
mappings.fails_here: Under amendment 1, the fresh-session review is the alternate path, taken after a crash or a full window. It is an exception, so it is rarely exercised and therefore untested at the moment it is needed. What the researcher read but did not write down can enter the review only as uncited judgment sentences, and no check covers those. My field cannot say which of the two writes better reviews; no source compares them for this job. It does say two things. The alternate must be exercised. The configuration in which every input to a checked output is recorded can be checked; the other cannot be.

mappings.classical: Acceptance sampling by attributes, with rectifying inspection. A sample whose result cannot reject the lot gives no protection.
solutions: Rectifying sampling inspection (a rejected lot is 100 % inspected; LTPD and AOQL plans) [Dodge, H.F. & Romig, H.G. (1929), 'A Method of Sampling Inspection', Bell System Technical Journal 8]
Sampling by attributes indexed by acceptance quality limit [ISO 2859-1, 'Sampling procedures for inspection by attributes']
mappings.rule: For each field and each reader's cards, draw a zero-acceptance sample (c = 0) of n cards that no conclusion cites. One semantic failure (wrong number or wrong conditions) means that reader's cards are all checked, or removed from the pack and listed as not covered. Amendment 3 turned the 95 % gate into a ledger measure with no action, and that removed the plan's protection.
mappings.runner: sample.js picks the cards with a recorded random seed. The fixed-brief checker checks them. The coordinator applies the result at gate A.
mappings.on_failure: Rectify the reader's cards (check them all) or quarantine them.
mappings.formula: Pa(p) = (1 - d*p)^n. Sample size for a lot tolerance p1 at consumer risk beta: n = ln(beta) / ln(1 - d*p1). Example: p1 = 0.10, beta = 0.10, d = 1 gives n = 22; d = 0.8 gives n = 28.
mappings.fails_here: Inspection is not perfect, so use the detection rate d measured in D4-01. Lots are not homogeneous: cards differ by reader and by type of source, so sample each reader separately. Sampling must be random by script, not left to the checker's choice. The 100 % check of cited cards is already the strongest plan for that critical subset. The open question is the cards no one cites. They still shape judgment, and they count toward coverage under P13.

mappings.classical: Use outside the assumed conditions: a correct component reused where its assumptions do not hold.
solutions: Lesson from Ariane 501: reused software whose assumptions were not checked against the new conditions [Lions, J.-L. et al. (1996), 'ARIANE 5 Flight 501 Failure: Report by the Inquiry Board']
Explicit context and assumption nodes in an assurance argument [Kelly, T.P. (1998), 'Arguing Safety: A Systematic Approach to Managing Safety Cases', PhD thesis, University of York]
mappings.rule: Card conditions are typed fields with a controlled vocabulary: task type, model family, repository size range, language, metric. Each citing sentence carries an applies_to record in the same fields. A script flags any applies_to value outside the card's range, and any condition the card has that the sentence leaves out (a dropped condition). Only flagged sentences, and conditions in free text, go to the model's judgment check.
mappings.runner: context-check.js, run by the coordinator after each review and after the synthesis.
mappings.on_failure: The sentence is marked 'outside conditions' and either relabelled as judgment or removed. The rate is recorded in the ledger.
mappings.formula: Pass when, for every field f: applies_to[f] is within card.conditions[f], and every f that is set on the card is also set on the sentence.
mappings.fails_here: Conditions are written in prose. Reviews paraphrase. Ranges ('repositories of 10k to 100k lines') rarely match the vocabulary of a claim. The field's answer is to make the precondition mechanical wherever the vocabulary allows, and to leave the model's judgment only for what remains.

mappings.classical: Qualifying a verifier by known-answer tests, with an oracle independent of the party being tested. Defects seeded into the material under review measure the reviewer.
solutions: Independent verification and validation (technical, managerial and financial independence) [IEEE Std 1012, 'Standard for System, Software, and Hardware Verification and Validation']
Error seeding applied to a reviewer [Mills, H.D. (1972), 'On the Statistical Validation of Computer Programs', IBM FSD report FSC-72-6015]

Perspective-based reading (inspectors with assigned perspectives, with measured detection) [Basili, V.R., Green, S., Laitenberger, O., Lanubile, F., Shull, F., Sorumgard, S., Zelkowitz, M.V. (1996), 'The Empirical Investigation of Perspective-Based Reading', Empirical Software Engineering 1(2)]
mappings.rule: Plant k = 2 to 4 known defects in the copies of our work that each expert is given. Each plant rests on a confirmed card. Examples: a design that assumes a result holds for a model or repository size that the card excludes; a quoted number that has been altered. At least one plant contradicts the answer we hope for, which tests for anchoring (P2). The expert is not told. Certification also requires that at least the owner's threshold of plants be found. The plants are then stripped from the review output using the key.
mappings.runner: The coordinator runs plant.js before the review and score-plants.js after it. The key is held outside every child's folder.
mappings.on_failure: An expert that misses every plant has its review labelled uncertified. One re-review is allowed from a fresh session (restart intensity 1, D4-07).
mappings.formula: With k plants and detection d, P(all found) = d^k. Pool across experts to estimate d for the programme: total found / total planted, with a Clopper-Pearson interval. Track the plant that runs against our hopes separately, as an anchoring rate.
mappings.fails_here: Technical independence is impossible within one model. A model may spot a plant as a plant. With 2 to 4 plants per expert, no rate can be estimated for one expert; the plants only catch gross failure. The rate can be pooled across experts for the programme as a whole. The current certification checks the expert's inputs (coverage, reading list, confirmed citations). It certifies the evidence, not the reviewer's ability to find what is wrong in our work.

mappings.classical: Closing a hazard log: a hazard, here a dismissal, may be closed only with verification evidence and acceptance by an independent party. Closures can be reopened.
solutions: Hazard tracking to closure, with verification evidence [MIL-STD-882E (2012), 'Department of Defense Standard Practice: System Safety']
mappings.rule: Every dismissal ('wrong form', 'wrong problem', a dropped field) is an entry in a log, with a reason class and the confirmed cards that show it. A dismissal without a confirmed card stays open, labelled 'judgment'. A new card that contradicts a dismissal reopens it. The refuter's input includes 2 or 3 seeded false dismissals of leads that confirmed cards support.
mappings.runner: A script builds the log from the review files. The refuter session attacks every entry. The coordinator closes only entries that have evidence.
mappings.on_failure: If the refuter misses the seeded dismissals, its 'upheld' verdicts are labelled unqualified, and those dismissals go to the owner as open entries.
mappings.formula: Refuter detection = seeded dismissals caught / seeded dismissals. Share of the log closed with evidence.
mappings.fails_here: The refuter is the same model as the reviewer that dismissed the lead (common mode, D4-02). Nobody knows the refuter's rate of misses. The field's answer is to require evidence for a closure and to measure the refuter by seeding.

missing.title: Detectors with no measured coverage: a count of zero failures read as quality
missing.classical: Latent faults in safety mechanisms; diagnostic coverage; proof testing (IEC 61508)
missing.mechanism: D4-01: blind seeding per fault class, with a proof-test seed in every wave.

missing.title: A check that could not run is counted as a pass
missing.classical: Fail-safe defaults; fail-open safety mechanism (Saltzer, J.H. & Schroeder, M.D. (1975), 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems', Proc. IEEE 63(9))
missing.mechanism: Every check returns pass, fail or not-run. Not-run is shown and counted, and is never treated as a pass. Gates count not-run against their threshold.

missing.title: The layers of defence fail together
missing.classical: Common-cause failure across layers of defence in depth (the 'Swiss cheese' model: Reason, J. (1990), 'Human Error', Cambridge University Press)
missing.mechanism: Measure the joint miss rate on seeded items across the layers in sequence (D4-02 formula, applied to layers). Report the measured end-to-end escape rate, not a product of rates.

missing.title: Single-version scripts as single points of failure
missing.classical: The voter or adjudicator as a single point of failure in N-version systems
missing.mechanism: Mutation-test each script before the pilot. Known-bad inputs (the seeded set of D4-01) must be rejected and known-good ones accepted. The test runs whenever a script changes.

missing.title: Gates become measures and drift is accepted
missing.classical: Normalization of deviance (Vaughan, D. (1996), 'The Challenger Launch Decision', University of Chicago Press)
missing.mechanism: Before the pilot, every ledger measure gets an action line set by the owner, and a script compares the measure with the line at each wave gate.

missing.title: Recovery and hand-over paths that never run
missing.classical: Untested alternates and failover paths (recovery-block alternates; latent faults in redundant paths)
missing.mechanism: Fault injection into the harness during the pilot: kill one child, put the PC to sleep once, force one coordinator hand-over, and record whether each path recovers.

missing.title: Recovery from a stale or inconsistent state
missing.classical: Inconsistent recovery point; a flaw in the controller's process model (STPA)
missing.mechanism: Status files carry a sequence number and a timestamp, and an older file is refused. Restore validation as in D4-07.

do_not: Do not take agreement between instances of one model as independent confirmation, and do not multiply their error rates as if they were independent (Knight & Leveson 1986).
Do not report a count of failed citations without the checker's measured detection rate: zero found is not zero present.
Do not let a check that could not run count as a pass.
Do not rely on checks at each hop in place of one end-to-end check against the source bytes. Checks at each hop only reduce how often the end-to-end check fails.
Do not turn a gate into a ledger measure unless an action threshold is fixed in advance.
Do not vote with two versions. Two can detect a fault, not decide it. Settle a disagreement with an acceptance test tied to the source.

Do not add redundancy (second experts, extra checkers, extra refuters) before its independence has been measured. Same-model redundancy adds cost and complexity and little coverage against design faults (Leveson 2011).
Do not let a checker learn which items are seeded or planted, or take its brief from the party it checks.
Do not keep a recovery path that never runs.
Do not restart a failed session again and again from the same inputs. After one restart, change the input or escalate.
Do not claim the problem list is complete. State the method, the model it rests on, and the estimated residual.
Do not check cards only after the review: an unchecked card in the expert's window shapes uncited judgment that no later check sees.

sources_with_a_problem.source: ISO 2859-1, Sampling procedures for inspection by attributes
sources_with_a_problem.correction: Cite as ISO 2859-1 (Part 1), with the AQL lot-by-lot subtitle and an edition year (1999 in my recall; a revision may exist).
sources_with_a_problem.note: Evidence: recalled description of the standard. The full title is 'Sampling procedures for inspection by attributes, Part 1: Sampling schemes indexed by acceptance quality limit (AQL) for lot-by-lot inspection'. Sample-size and acceptance-number tables are right. The cited title omits the part number and subtitle, and no edition year is given.

result.check_overall: I did not open any source. Every check rests on my recall of bibliographic records and standard textbook descriptions, and I say so in each note. All 37 citations point to real works, and authors, years and venues match. Two entries have a bibliographic gap (ISO 2859-1 title and edition, MIL-STD-1629A cancelled in 1998). Several claims are stated too strongly. Mills' estimate is unbiased only under the equal-detectability assumption. Randell's domino-effect condition is narrower than the full recovery-line treatment. Knight and Leveson traced coincident faults to more than the specification. Perspective-based reading evidence for different perspectives finding different defects is mixed. The restart-intensity wording in the Armstrong item is OTP behaviour, and I am unsure the thesis states it that way. The supervision-tree and GSN mapping in D4-whole is the design's own analogy. Nothing was marked could_not_check, but a pass that fetched the sources would be firmer on page numbers, clause numbers and exact wording.

whole.name: The Clark-Wilson commercial integrity model, enforced by a small reference monitor, with Biba-style integrity labels propagated through the work (process-granularity information-flow control in the style of Flume)
whole.source: D. D. Clark and D. R. Wilson, 1987, 'A Comparison of Commercial and Military Computer Security Policies', IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy; K. J. Biba, 1977, 'Integrity Considerations for Secure Computer Systems', MITRE MTR-3153; J. P. Anderson, 1972, 'Computer Security Technology Planning Study', ESD-TR-73-51 (the reference monitor); M. Krohn et al., 2007, 'Information Flow Control for Standard OS Abstractions', SOSP (Flume)
whole.borrow: (1) An integrity status field on every file, which only an IVP script may write and which lives in a folder the producer cannot write. Values: UDI, CDI-confirmed, CDI-judgment. The author never sets it. (2) The enforcement rules. A session's tool and write permissions are its certified triples: readers return values only; a child writes only its own folder; checkers return an enum verdict; only the merge script, run by the coordinator, writes shared paths. (3) Rule C5 as a gate. Nothing downstream (pack freeze, synthesis, the owner's table) may read an item whose status is UDI. (4) Separation of duty. The producer of an item never briefs, runs or chooses its verifier. (5) An append-only log written by the harness or a script, never by the subject (C4). (6) IVPs run on a schedule and at every restart, not only once (the Clark-Wilson IVP certifies that a CDI is still valid).

mappings.classical: Using unvalidated input to build trusted data: a Clark-Wilson C5 violation. The current rule checks after the review, which is an audit, not a gate.
solutions: Clark-Wilson CDI/UDI with rule C5 (a UDI is turned into a CDI only by a certified TP) and IVPs [Clark and Wilson, 1987, 'A Comparison of Commercial and Military Computer Security Policies', IEEE S&P]
mappings.rule: Every card, pack, review and synthesis row carries a status (UDI / CDI-confirmed / CDI-judgment) held in a status file that only the check script writes. A review is UDI until every card it cites is CDI-confirmed and every citing sentence has passed the within-conditions check. The synthesis script and pack freeze read only CDI items and refuse UDI. Conditions are not summarised: the synthesis script copies the card's condition fields by reference (card id plus field), so they cannot fall off.
mappings.runner: A Node script (check-status.mjs) run by the watcher after each card batch and after each review; the synthesis script enforces the read rule
mappings.on_failure: The item stays UDI. Pack freeze and synthesis exit non-zero listing the UDI ids, so the field cannot advance a gate. The count goes to the ledger.
mappings.formula: status(card) = CDI-confirmed iff schema_ok AND quote_found_in_snapshot AND checker_verdict = confirmed AND hash(card) = hash at verdict. status(review sentence) = min over cited cards. status(review) = UDI if any factual sentence has status UDI.
mappings.fails_here: LLM checkers cannot be certified. Only scripts can. The review is written before its cited cards are confirmed, so the trusted object (the review) temporarily depends on UDIs. Clark-Wilson tolerates this only if the derived object itself stays UDI until every input is validated.

mappings.classical: The confused deputy (indirect prompt injection is its LLM instance): a principal holding authority acts on instructions from a party who lacks that authority. Least privilege and privilege separation are the standard remedies.
solutions: Confused deputy; capabilities instead of ambient authority [N. Hardy, 1988, 'The Confused Deputy (or why capabilities might have been invented)', ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review]
Least privilege, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation [J. H. Saltzer and M. D. Schroeder, 1975, 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems', Proceedings of the IEEE]

Privilege separation: the part that parses untrusted input holds no privilege and talks to the privileged part through a narrow typed interface [N. Provos, M. Friedl and P. Honeyman, 2003, 'Preventing Privilege Escalation', USENIX Security]

Indirect prompt injection as the LLM threat; capability and data-flow separation as defence (CaMeL) [K. Greshake et al., 2023, 'Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection', AISec; E. Debenedetti et al., 2025, 'Defeating Prompt Injections by Design' (arXiv; the checker should verify the author list)]
mappings.rule: (1) Readers: no Read, Write, Bash or git tools; web only; their brief holds no project data. (2) Card free text is narrowed. Numbers, enums, ids and URLs are typed. 'What was measured' and 'conditions' are each capped (about 40 words). The quote is at most 15 words and must be found by the quote script in the snapshot (D5-04). (3) The child never reads raw web text itself. Reading an original is done by a no-tool helper that returns typed extracts, the dual-model pattern. If the owner wants the child to read originals, the child's label drops (D5-06) and its review is UDI until fully checked. (4) The child's authority is minimal and set outside its reach. Its write is allowed only under fields/<n>-<name>/ in its worktree. No shell, no MCP connectors, no network except via helpers, no git push; the merge script commits. Deny rules live in user- or managed-level settings, not in the worktree. (5) Before each wave, a script diffs the child's effective permission set against the profile.
mappings.runner: The coordinator sets the permission profile at session start; a Node script (perm-audit.mjs) reads each transcript after the turn and lists any tool call outside the profile
mappings.on_failure: Any out-of-profile call or write outside the folder: the child's branch is quarantined (not merged), its outputs are marked UDI, the watcher exits and wakes the coordinator, and the owner is told
mappings.formula: Permitted(session, tool, path) is a fixed table; audit = set(tool calls in transcript) minus Permitted, which must be empty.
mappings.fails_here: In an LLM, data and instructions share one channel, so a string field in a valid card can still carry instructions. The schema check is a type check, not a taint barrier. The child is the deputy: it holds write tools, git and helper spawning, and it also reads originals of must-read sources directly and the free-text fields of cards. The current rule de-privileges the reader, which was already the least dangerous party, and leaves the deputy exposed. Permissions written in the child's own worktree (.claude/settings.json) are modifiable by the child. The field's answer when the separation cannot be made perfect is to bound authority so that a steered deputy can do little damage, and to keep untrusted text away from the planner.

mappings.classical: Information-flow control and taint tracking: the trust label of derived data must be computed from its inputs, and labels must survive every hand-over
solutions: Lattice model of information flow [D. E. Denning, 1976, 'A Lattice Model of Secure Information Flow', Communications of the ACM]
Decentralized label model with explicit endorsement and declassification [A. C. Myers and B. Liskov, 1997, 'A Decentralized Model for Information Flow Control', SOSP]
Process-granularity IFC: a process's label is the combination of everything it has read [M. Krohn et al., 2007, 'Information Flow Control for Standard OS Abstractions', SOSP (Flume)]
mappings.rule: A label lattice: replicated > independent > single study > vendor's own > unconfirmed > judgment. Each claim in a review or the synthesis gets label = min(cited card labels). A session gets label_session = min(labels of all items it read), taken from the transcript. A verdict (judgment) carries min(label of its supporting claims, label_session). The checker's confirmation is the only endorsement point. The synthesis script prints each claim with its label and the card's condition fields, so caveats travel mechanically.
mappings.runner: The synthesis script and a label script over transcripts and review.json
mappings.on_failure: A claim whose label is below the threshold the owner sets cannot appear as a finding; it is listed as judgment or open
mappings.formula: label(claim) = min_{c in cites(claim)} label(c); label(session) = min_{x in reads(session)} label(x); label(verdict) = min(label of its claims, label(session)).
mappings.fails_here: An LLM's output depends on its whole window. Every sentence is an implicit flow from everything it read, so sentence-level labels from citations understate the taint. The field's answer, when internal flows cannot be tracked, is coarse-grained labelling at the process boundary (Flume): the session is labelled by what it read, from the harness transcript.

mappings.classical: The verification depends on a component outside the trusted computing base, which sits in the attacker's channel: the summarising small model. Remedies: reference monitor and TCB minimisation, plus TOCTOU binding of check to use.
solutions: Reference monitor: always invoked, tamper-proof, small enough to be verified [J. P. Anderson, 1972, 'Computer Security Technology Planning Study', ESD-TR-73-51]
Economy of mechanism and complete mediation [Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975, 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems', Proc. IEEE]
Time-of-check-to-time-of-use races [M. Bishop and M. Dilger, 1996, 'Checking for Race Conditions in File Accesses', Computing Systems]
mappings.rule: The quote script fetches the address itself, with no rendering and no script execution. It stores the bytes as a content-addressed snapshot (sha256), extracts text, normalises whitespace, case, Unicode quotes and hyphens, and searches for the quote. On a hit it records (card hash, snapshot hash, offset) and a window of about 200 words around it. The checker is then given that window from the snapshot, not a live fetch. A card edited after the check, or a re-fetch whose hash differs, voids the confirmation. A PDF or a blocked page is labelled 'not machine-checkable' (one rank below confirmed); it is never passed.
mappings.runner: quote-check.mjs, run by the watcher on each new card batch
mappings.on_failure: Quote not found: the card stays UDI and cannot be cited. Unfetchable: labelled 'not machine-checkable'. The ledger counts both.
mappings.formula: confirmed_quote = normalise(quote) is a substring of normalise(text(snapshot)), with confirmation bound to (sha256(card), sha256(snapshot)).
mappings.fails_here: Pages change between fetches, sit behind paywalls, are PDFs, or render with scripts, so a plain-Node fetch may not see the text. A page is attacker-controlled: it can contain any string, so 'quote found' proves only that the string is on the page, not that it supports the claim. The field's answer is to bind the check to an immutable snapshot (hash) and to treat 'not machine-checkable' as its own lower label, never as passed.

mappings.classical: Separation of duty whose two parties are not independent (correlated failure, the equivalent of collusion), and design diversity
solutions: Separation of duty (Clark-Wilson); separation of privilege [Clark and Wilson, 1987, IEEE S&P; Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975, Proc. IEEE]
N-version programming [A. Avizienis, 1985, 'The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering]

Measured refutation of the independence assumption [J. C. Knight and N. G. Leveson, 1986, 'An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering]
mappings.rule: Order of preference for each check. (1) A deterministic script (quote, number-in-window regex, schema). (2) A different model family, if F3 allows. (3) A same-model checker that sees only the snapshot window and the citing sentence, never the producer's reasoning or brief, with a verdict from a fixed enum. (4) An owner spot-check of a random sample of confirmed items. Agreement between same-model instances adds nothing (current P3 rule kept). F2: a second reviewer of the same frozen pack shares the pack's errors, and a second research run shares the model's; neither is independent. Security prefers whichever adds a different model or different inputs; with one model, the contrary-evidence reader (different input) is the diverse part.
mappings.runner: The check script decides the tier per item; the coordinator draws the owner sample with a seeded random script
mappings.on_failure: A judgment check from tier 3 only gives the label CDI-judgment, never CDI-confirmed
mappings.formula: Estimate checker miss rate m from seeded faults (D5-14). With correlated same-model checks, P(both miss) is about m, not m squared; budget as if one check.
mappings.fails_here: Instances of one model are the worst case of Knight and Leveson: same training, so correlated blind spots. Separation of duty between two instances is separation of process, not of judgment. The field's answer: make the check deterministic where possible (scripts), force diversity where not (a different model family, different inputs, a human sample), and never treat agreement as independent confirmation.

mappings.classical: Biba strict integrity ('no read down'), or the low-water-mark policy: a subject that has read low-integrity data may not produce high-integrity data
solutions: Biba strict integrity and the low-water-mark policy [K. J. Biba, 1977, 'Integrity Considerations for Secure Computer Systems', MITRE MTR-3153]
mappings.rule: From an integrity standpoint the review is written by a fresh session whose only reads are the frozen pack (hash verified), snapshot windows of must-read sections, and our files. Its label_session is then CDI. The researcher may hand over a typed gaps file: questions and card requests only, no claims. Those go back through readers and the checker before the reviewer may see them. If the owner keeps the same-session review (amendment 1), its verdicts are labelled at the researcher's low-water mark and every factual sentence must pass D5-01 before use. Same-session verdicts then count as judgment in the synthesis.
mappings.runner: The coordinator starts the reviewer with a read allowlist; the label script checks the transcript's reads against it
mappings.on_failure: A read outside the allowlist drops the review's label to UDI, and it is re-run or fully checked
mappings.formula: label(review) = min over reads(reviewer); fresh reviewer = CDI if reads is a subset of {pack, snapshots, our files}
mappings.fails_here: The researcher's extra knowledge, what it read but did not write down, is by definition unlabelled and unchecked, and the integrity model has no way to credit it. Under Biba, unverifiable input is low integrity. The researcher's window holds dropped cards, raw originals and possibly injected text. A fresh session that reads only the frozen pack, which is all CDIs, plus the must-read sections from snapshots, keeps its label at CDI level. Whether the lost unwritten knowledge costs quality is outside this field: the pilot measures it.

mappings.classical: Assurance by evaluating evidence, not trusting self-assessment. Integrity attaches to outputs (Clark-Wilson certifies data and procedures, not a subject's competence); a trusted audit trail records what the subject actually did.
solutions: Output certification via IVPs; logging by the system (rule C4) [Clark and Wilson, 1987, IEEE S&P]
mappings.rule: Keep the current rule, which is Clark-Wilson's stance, with two tightenings. (1) 'What it read' is taken from the harness transcript (tool calls and returned card ids), never from the session's own ledger lines. (2) The certificate is a script output listing: approved question ids covered by at least one CDI-confirmed card; reads matched against the input list; every cited card CDI and within conditions (from D5-01); verdicts resting only on vendor or single-study cards labelled judgment. No line of the certificate is written by the session.
mappings.runner: certify.mjs, run by the coordinator's watcher at gate B
mappings.on_failure: An uncovered question id is marked 'not covered' in the synthesis. Reads off-list or any UDI citation mean the review is not admitted.
mappings.formula: coverage = |{q : there is a CDI-confirmed card answering q}| / |Q|
mappings.fails_here: Whether 'the session knows its field' is a property of its window, which cannot be audited. Only its outputs and its read trace can be. Coverage of question ids is checkable; depth of understanding is not, so the field says not to claim it.

mappings.classical: Tamper-proofness of the TCB: the subject must not be able to modify its own checker, policy or audit tools
solutions: Reference monitor tamper-proofness [J. P. Anderson, 1972, ESD-TR-73-51]
File integrity checking by hash baseline [G. H. Kim and E. H. Spafford, 1994, 'The Design and Implementation of Tripwire: A File System Integrity Checker', ACM CCS]
mappings.rule: Schemas, scripts, checker briefs, question lists and permission profiles live in the coordinator's checkout at a pinned commit, and their hashes are recorded in the ledger. Every check runs from there, never from a child's worktree. The merge script is the only TP that moves a child's work into the shared tree. It rejects any branch whose diff touches a path outside fields/<n>-<name>/ (a path allowlist, which also enforces P6's one writer per folder) and verifies the TCB hashes before running.
mappings.runner: merge.mjs, run by the coordinator
mappings.on_failure: Merge refused; the branch is quarantined; the watcher exits with the reason
mappings.formula: accept iff changed_paths are within the child's allowed prefix AND sha256(TCB files) = baseline
mappings.fails_here: A git worktree holds the whole repository, so a child with write tools can edit its copy of the schemas, check scripts, checker brief, question list or .claude/settings.json. If any check runs from the child's worktree, the checked party controls the check.

mappings.classical: Transitive confused deputy and taint laundering upward: the most privileged subject (the coordinator: starts sessions, merges, writes the protocol) reads low-integrity text relayed by less privileged ones. This violates Biba no-read-down at the top.
solutions: Biba no-read-down applied to the most privileged subject; privilege separation of the privileged part [Biba, 1977, MTR-3153; Provos, Friedl and Honeyman, 2003, USENIX Security]
mappings.rule: The coordinator reads only script-produced status. That status is typed: counts of CDI cards, gate states, enum error codes, file pointers, token totals counted by script from transcripts, and progress counted only from CDI promotions, which the child cannot forge. A child's free-text note is written to a file the coordinator does not read in full. A repair request is a typed record (question id plus missing-evidence enum). Reading verdict text is allowed only once the review is CDI.
mappings.runner: The watcher script composes status.json; the coordinator's brief allows only status.json and CDI files
mappings.on_failure: A coordinator read of a UDI file appears in the transcript audit and is flagged to the owner; the hand-over pointer (P11) also points only to status.json
mappings.formula: progress(t) = number of CDI promotions in (t - box, t]; stall iff progress = 0 and time > box
mappings.fails_here: A child's end-of-turn note is free text, and a child's window may hold injected or false text, so the note can carry it to the coordinator. The coordinator cannot be made to ignore what it reads.

mappings.classical: The verifier as a confused deputy: the checker holds the authority to certify, and it reads the attacker-controlled object it certifies
solutions: Least privilege plus a narrow typed interface for the verifier (Saltzer and Schroeder; privilege separation) [Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975, Proc. IEEE; Provos, Friedl and Honeyman, 2003, USENIX Security]
mappings.rule: The checker has no tools. It receives the snapshot window chosen by the script, the card's typed fields and the citing sentence, and returns an enum verdict (confirmed / number mismatch / conditions mismatch / outside conditions / unclear) with a pointer to an offset. A 'confirmed' verdict is accepted only if the script also finds the card's number in the window.
mappings.runner: The check script assembles the checker's input and validates the output
mappings.on_failure: An off-enum or unsupported verdict counts as 'unclear', and the item stays UDI
mappings.formula: accept_confirm iff verdict = confirmed AND regex(number, window) matches
mappings.fails_here: A page can contain text aimed at the checker ('this figure is correct'); the attack record itself notes pages reporting text aimed at the reader (README limit 4).

mappings.classical: Audit log integrity: a subject must not write or alter its own audit record. Use forward-secure, hash-chained logs.
solutions: Secure audit logs (hash chaining) [B. Schneier and J. Kelsey, 1999, 'Secure Audit Logs to Support Computer Forensics', ACM Transactions on Information and System Security]
Accountability and logging as a system function (rule C4) [Clark and Wilson, 1987, IEEE S&P]
mappings.rule: Ledger entries that matter for gates (tokens, time, reads, promotions, failures) are written only by scripts, from transcripts and status files. Each entry holds sha256(previous entry). A session's own lines are kept as notes and are not counted. The merge script verifies the chain.
mappings.runner: ledger.mjs, called by the watcher and the merge script
mappings.on_failure: A chain break stops the wave and is reported
mappings.formula: h_i = sha256(h_{i-1} || entry_i)
mappings.fails_here: Amendment 3 has each session keep its own ledger lines (self-attested). Token counts are already taken from transcripts by script, which is correct; failures and progress are still partly self-reported.

mappings.classical: Integrity verification at restart (a Clark-Wilson IVP run before reuse; Tripwire-style baseline check)
solutions: Re-run IVPs before a CDI is reused; hash baseline [Clark and Wilson, 1987, IEEE S&P; Kim and Spafford, 1994, ACM CCS]
mappings.rule: A fresh session is given the pack only if sha256(pack) equals the frozen hash in the ledger. Restarting from cards uses only CDI-confirmed rows; partial or UDI rows go back to the checker.
mappings.runner: restart.mjs, run by the coordinator before starting the replacement
mappings.on_failure: Hash mismatch: no restart, and the coordinator is woken with the reason
mappings.formula: start iff sha256(pack) = ledger.pack_hash
mappings.fails_here: A crash can leave a half-written cards.jsonl; a restart 'from cards' may read UDI or truncated rows.

mappings.classical: Threat enumeration by systematic modelling: per-element STRIDE over a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries; attack trees
solutions: STRIDE threat modelling per DFD element [L. Kohnfelder and P. Garg, 1999, 'The Threats to Our Products', Microsoft (internal); A. Shostack, 2014, 'Threat Modeling: Designing for Security', Wiley]
Attack trees [B. Schneier, 1999, 'Attack Trees', Dr. Dobb's Journal]
mappings.rule: One session draws the DFD: coordinator, child, reader, checker, reviewer, scripts, files, web, owner, with trust boundaries (web to reader, reader to child, child to coordinator, session to repository). It fills a matrix of elements by {spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege, confident falsehood, anchoring, stall}. Each cell holds a problem id or 'n/a: reason'. A script checks that no cell is empty and that every problem id appears in at least one cell.
mappings.runner: One fresh Opus session writes it; check-matrix.mjs validates; the refuter attacks the 'n/a' cells
mappings.on_failure: An empty cell blocks the pilot; a new threat gets an id and a handling row
mappings.formula: cells = |elements| x |threat classes|; all must be filled
mappings.fails_here: STRIDE is aimed at adversaries; here most faults are non-malicious (false confidence, stalls). Add the fault classes from 'Faults' as extra columns. The field never claims completeness; it claims a checked enumeration.

mappings.classical: Measuring a defence's detection rate by fault seeding and red-team canaries, rather than assuming it
solutions: Error seeding to estimate the fraction of faults that escape detection [H. D. Mills, 1972, 'On the Statistical Validation of Computer Programs', IBM Federal Systems Division report (the checker should verify the title)]
mappings.rule: In the pilot, a script inserts k planted cards: invented source, wrong number, wrong conditions, and an out-of-conditions citing sentence. It also points one reader at a local canary page carrying injected instructions, the owner's own test file. Detection is measured at each IVP. Plants are tagged in a sealed file that the checkers cannot read.
mappings.runner: seed.mjs, run by the coordinator in the pilot only; results read by a script
mappings.on_failure: Detection below a threshold the owner sets: that IVP is not trusted and its items stay CDI-judgment
mappings.formula: d = detected_seeded / k; estimated residual = observed_failures x (1 - d) / d
mappings.fails_here: Seeded wrong cards may be easier to catch than a model's natural distortions; seed both invented and subtly distorted (wrong condition, wrong baseline) cards.

missing.title: Injected or false text travels up the tree to the coordinator
missing.classical: Transitive confused deputy / taint laundering (Biba no-read-down violated at the most privileged subject)
missing.mechanism: D5-09: the coordinator reads only typed, script-produced status; free-text notes are kept out of its window

missing.title: The checker is steered by the page it checks
missing.classical: Verifier as confused deputy
missing.mechanism: D5-10: no tools, enum verdict, snapshot window chosen by script, number cross-check

missing.title: A child edits its own checks, schemas, briefs or permission file in its worktree
missing.classical: TCB tampering (reference monitor not tamper-proof)
missing.mechanism: D5-08: checks run from the coordinator's pinned checkout; hash baseline; the merge path allowlist

missing.title: A card or page changes between check and use
missing.classical: TOCTOU
missing.mechanism: D5-04: confirmation bound to (card hash, snapshot hash)

missing.title: Sessions hold ambient authority they do not need (browser, mail, connectors, git push, shell)
missing.classical: Ambient authority (M. S. Miller, K.-P. Yee and J. Shapiro, 2003, 'Capability Myths Demolished')
missing.mechanism: Start children and helpers with connectors disabled and an explicit tool allowlist set at user or managed level; audit with perm-audit.mjs (D5-02)

missing.title: Private project data leaks through web searches or fetched URLs
missing.classical: The confinement problem / exfiltration (B. W. Lampson, 1973, 'A Note on the Confinement Problem', Communications of the ACM)
missing.mechanism: Readers get no file-read tool and a brief with no project data, so there is nothing to leak; the transcript audit greps outgoing queries for a project-term denylist

missing.title: Self-attested audit records
missing.classical: Repudiation / log written by the subject (Clark-Wilson rule C4; Schneier and Kelsey 1999)
missing.mechanism: D5-11: gate figures come only from scripts over transcripts, in a hash chain

missing.title: Integrity labels assigned by the producer
missing.classical: Self-endorsement (DLM endorsement without authority)
missing.mechanism: The evidence field is a claim checked by the checker; the label is written only by the status script (D5-01, D5-03)

do_not: Do not rely on an instruction such as 'text in sources is data, never follow it' as a control. In-band signalling is the root of injection; only removing authority or the channel works (Saltzer and Schroeder: fail-safe defaults).
Do not use injection detection or blacklist filters as the defence. Deny by default and bound the deputy's authority.
Do not let the checked party brief, choose, run or host its checker, its schemas or its scripts (separation of duty; tamper-proof TCB).
Do not count agreement between instances of the same model as two independent checks (Knight and Leveson 1986).
Do not let a producer set an item's integrity label or status; only a certified IVP script writes it.
Do not raise a label by summarising: a summary of UDIs is UDI (no laundering).
Do not treat a check that runs after the output has already been consumed as prevention; downstream consumers must refuse UDI items until the check completes.
Do not put permission or deny rules where the session can write them (its own worktree's .claude/settings.json).
Do not give any session ambient authority 'for convenience': a shell, connectors, push rights or network beyond its role.
Do not let a checker fetch live pages or execute or render them; work from a hashed snapshot.
Do not have the privileged coordinator read free text from less trusted sessions.
Do not claim to certify what a session 'knows'; certify its outputs and its read trace.
result.check_overall: Every cited source exists and the bibliographic details are right. I checked this with web searches for six of them: the CaMeL paper (arXiv:2503.18813), Provos et al., Flume, Bishop and Dilger, and the Mills seeding report. The rest I accepted from standard bibliographic knowledge, which I did not fetch pages to confirm. The weaker points are about what is claimed, not whether the source exists. (1) Bishop and Dilger is about detecting TOCTTOU flaws, not about hash binding as a fix. (2) Biba's strict integrity prevents contamination, while the low-water-mark policy lowers the subject's level instead. (3) Schneier and Kelsey give forward integrity only, so entries written after the log host is compromised are not protected. (4) CaMeL's guarantee is shown on AgentDojo, at a utility cost, and depends on correct policies and excludes side channels. (5) Clark-Wilson assumes certified TPs and IVPs, so the structural defence holds only if those are deterministic code the agents cannot change. (6) The 1997 decentralized label model is mainly about declassification, and endorsement comes from later work. (7) The Mills report is an internal IBM document that I could confirm only through secondary citations, and the Kohnfelder and Garg memo is similar.

result.field: Statistics, experimental design, ensemble learning and evidence synthesis

whole.name: A systematic review with GRADE certainty ratings, run in its rapid-review form, with the synthesis across fields done as an overview of reviews
whole.source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (Higgins and Thomas, eds.); PRISMA-P (Moher et al. 2015, 'Preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015 statement', Systematic Reviews); PRISMA 2020 (Page et al. 2021, 'The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews', BMJ); PRISMA-S (Rethlefsen et al. 2021, 'PRISMA-S: an extension to the PRISMA Statement for Reporting Literature Searches in Systematic Reviews', Systematic Reviews); GRADE (Guyatt et al. 2008, 'GRADE: an emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations', BMJ); GRADE Evidence to Decision frameworks (Alonso-Coello et al. 2016, BMJ). Rapid-review guidance: Cochrane Rapid Reviews Methods Group (Garritty et al. 2021, J Clin Epidemiol); the authors and title of this one should be checked.
